Should We All Be Seeing a Concierge Doctor?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • In a recent development, for as long as I can remember, going to my primary care doctor has been simple: I’d schedule an appointment a few weeks (or months) in advance, commute across town for an in-person appointment, and hope that my insurance covered whatever labs were ordered.
  • According to recent reports, over the past few years, the number of concierge medicine services like Tia and One Medical has skyrocketed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, for as long as I can remember, going to my primary care doctor has been simple: I’d schedule an appointment a few weeks (or months) in advance, commute across town for an in-person appointment, and hope that my insurance covered whatever labs were ordered. But lately, many people have been opting for a membership-based system where they pay a monthly or annual fee for on-demand care. This concept is called concierge medicine.

According to recent reports, over the past few years, the number of concierge medicine services like Tia and One Medical has skyrocketed. Between 2018 and 2023, the number of direct primary care and concierge practice sites grew by roughly 83 percent, per a 2025 study in Health Affairs. (But there are also concierge practices specific to gynecology, longevity medicine, and even emergency medicine.).

“Over the course of my career, I've seen a lot of frustrations that patients have had in terms of access to care, long wait times, lack of continuity of care,” says Jane Zhu, MD, a primary care provider and associate professor of medicine at Oregon Health and Science University, and author of the Health Affairs study. There’s a real need for faster, more on-demand medical care—and concierge medicine is one way that patients are getting that.

Membership prices vary, with some costing as little as $9 a month for on-demand urgent and primary care, and others costing as much as $45,000 a year for top-tier care (at-home doctor visits for urgent care, X-ray imaging from your bed, and even private jets on standby for medical evacuation while you’re traveling). If you don’t live in a major city, many of these programs offer telehealth services all over the country.

So, what’s the catch? Ahead, read up on everything you need to know about concierge medicine, including the pros and cons, and who it’s right for.

The premise is simple: paying a membership fee unlocks extra attention and access to care from your doctor.

At most traditional clinics and hospitals, the goal is for doctors to see as many patients a day as possible. (More visits equals more insurance claims and/or copays, which in turn makes money for the practice.) With concierge medicine, doctors don’t operate within this same construct. Instead, they make money from membership fees, which means they can still turn a profit with a much smaller pool of patients. When you schedule an appointment with a concierge doctor, you’re not competing with hundreds of other patients for a time slot in the same way you would for a traditional doctor.

When Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai, worked in traditional medicine, she only got about 15 to 20 minutes for each patient visit. Now, she has the freedom to extend her visits to 45 to 60 minutes and form closer relationships with her patients. “I'm able to go into deeper discussions from a more holistic perspective and have a different type of conversation,” she notes. Talking more in depth about sleep, nutrition, and lifestyle habits in general is key to helping her patients prevent illnesses in the first place—not just treat them when they come up.

According to recent reports, additionally, getting lab work done through concierge medicine may be a smoother process. While some traditional practices may have you drop by LabCorp to get your blood drawn, for example, many concierge practices will just do it on site, and even go beyond your average complete blood count for in-depth lipid, hormone, and genetic panels. But everything isn't always included in the membership, so check before they draw.

When you need a specialist outside of your concierge practice, they’ll often have health navigators—people whose job it is to schedule your appointments for you, facilitate communication between your providers, coordinate prescriptions, and run point on any insurance claims. Because the health care system can feel so fragmented and hard to understand, the health navigation piece is a major highlight for many patients, indicates Scott Braunstein, MD, an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care.

According to recent reports, regarding costs outside of the membership fee and bloodwork, every concierge practice is different. At Tia, for example, preventative care services like yearly physicals or vaccinations are usually covered by insurance, but diagnostic appointments often come with additional out-of-pocket fees. That means that if you come in for a UTI, sick visit, or complaint about a latest health problem, it’ll often result in an additional charge on the patient’s end. The average copay for these kinds of visits at Tia is between $15 and $75—not too different from a traditional doctor’s appointment. However, at a high-end program where you pay entirely out of pocket, the care is pretty all-inclusive.

As of now, there isn’t enough data on concierge medicine to determine whether this model provides superior health outcomes for patients—like fewer hospitalizations or better chronic disease management—compared to traditional systems. That being said, there is one undeniable factor that contributes to good health: regularly going to the doctor. A 2026 report by the health policy initiative Milbank Memorial Fund found that people with chronic illnesses who regularly see a primary care provider have lower rates of hospitalization and emergency room visits—and lower health care costs on the whole.

However, in the U.S., about one-third of adults don’t have a usual source of primary care, per the report. Concierge medicine is one way to bridge this gap of primary care access, and give people an easy, on-demand way to take care of their health. Appointments are easier to schedule, can often be taken from your phone or computer, and the experience is designed to just be more enjoyable and convenient. “When we remove barriers for people accessing care, people are more likely to engage in their health. And when people are more likely to engage in their health, they have better health outcomes,” notes Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the vice president of In-Office Care at One Medical.

Sources indicate that if you can get into these models of care, they seem to be beneficial for both the clinician and the patient. But the question remains: “What happens if you can't get into those models of care?” says Dr. Zhu.

Industry observers note that the number of clinicians practicing in membership-based clinics grew by 78 percent between 2018 and 2023, per the Health Affairs study. That means that more clinicians are leaving traditional medicine for this model—which could put pressure on an already-stretched-thin primary care system. If more clinicians leave the traditional system, it could become harder for the people who can’t pay for concierge medicine to access the traditional care they need. So while concierge medicine may help some people live healthier lives, it doesn’t yet fix the broader need for more primary care access in the United States, indicates Dr. Zhu.

In a recent development, the study also found that while concierge medicine providers are growing, the share of physicians actually declined, and the number of advanced practice providers—like nurses, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants—increased. These advanced practice providers were more likely to be fresh entrants to the workforce with no prior employer. So while there are still concierge providers with a career’s worth of experience, you might be more likely to get a newer provider with less experience if you opt for concierge medicine.

If you’re frustrated with a fragmented health system where you have to be the one to connect the dots between all of your doctors, concierge medicine could be a welcome reprieve. For instance, Dr. Harvey expects to see more and more patients with chronic illnesses opting for concierge models in the next couple of years. If you have a condition like PMOS, for example, you might be seeing five different specialists to deal with the symptoms: a dermatologist, endocrinologist, gynecologist, nutritionist, and a primary care provider.

Industry observers note that with a concierge practice that specializes in convenient, wraparound care, you may be able to see multiple of these specialists all in one place, and have a health navigator or coach to help you coordinate appointments, claims Dr. Bhuyan. When you’re dealing with complex medical conditions, or just finding yourself going to the doctor a lot for illnesses or infections, paying for extra time and access to your doctor might just make for a better experience.

The term “concierge” can make this form of care seem cost-prohibitive—and some services certainly are. That said, there are a few options with low membership fees that take insurance, including One Medical (starting at $9/month), Sesame Plus ($10.99/month), Tia Signature ($25-a-month membership, only available in some states) and Folx ($44/month).

According to recent reports, if you’re using insurance, you’ll have to do your research to determine how much you’ll pay out of pocket. Popular services like Tia, Allara, Folx, and One Medical accept a wide variety of insurance prepares, but specify that copays and other fees can vary plan by plan, just like at the regular doctor. If you’re not using insurance, these practices usually specify self-pay costs in addition to the membership fee depending on the visit or service type, and depending on the care you’re looking for, it could be a bargain.

According to recent reports, before committing to a membership anywhere, find out which services will and won’t be covered (like lab testing or imaging), and how easy it is to cancel noted membership if you decide it’s not a fit, claims Dr. Bhuyan.

According to recent reports, A lot of times, you can also find local doctors practicing concierge-style medicine, and there are search tools like MDVIP or NextMD, which connect patients with a network of in-person concierge physicians all over the country. And if you can’t find one near you, there are plenty of large-scale telehealth services at your fingertips. Be sure to research the doctor beforehand to make sure that they’re legit, and that their expertise aligns with your goals, notes Dr. Bhuyan.

Overall, health care is shifting more towards patients’ autonomy. They want to “decide how their health care dollars are spent, whether that's through HSA plans or other means. They’re more empowered to choose the service that works for them,” states Dr. Braunstein. So, only you can decide if a concierge doctor is right for you (and your wallet!).

In a recent development, meet the experts: Jane Zhu, MD, is a primary care provider and Associate Professor of Medicine at Oregon Health and Science University. Kristen Harvey, MD, MPH, is a concierge family medicine physician at Mount Sinai. Scott Braunstein, MD, is an internal and emergency medicine physician and the chief medical officer at Sollis Health, a concierge clinic for urgent and emergency care. Natasha Bhuyan, MD, is a primary care provider and the Vice President of In-Office Care at One Medical, a membership-based in-person and telehealth clinic owned by Amazon.

Iceland’s first wind farm comes with a water-saving bonus

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.
  • Industry observers note that vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads.
  • Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power company, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.

Industry observers note that vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads. And Iceland’s windiest months coincide with the time of year when less water flows into its reservoirs.

Landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power company, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026. The first 14 turbines are online; another 14 will be installed in a second phase, and the entire wind farm is expected to be operating by the end of 2027.

Once complete, Vaðölduver will have 120 megawatts (MW) of capacity. When I met with the folks at Landsvirkjun in Reykjavik last month, they told me that’s enough to power the equivalent of 90,000 Icelandic households. Vaðalda’s electricity feeds into the grid and is sold through power purchase agreements.

Vaðölduver sits on a lava-and-sand plain east of the Þjórsá River, south of Sultartangi Dam. Landsvirkjun already operates seven hydropower stations in the surrounding Þjórsá and Tungnaá region.

The wind farm was sited in this region of Iceland because the seasons line up nicely.

It has been revealed that the winds are strongest in winter, when inflows into hydropower reservoirs can be low. In summer, wind speeds tend to drop, but glacial melt increases water availability for the hydropower system.

When the wind turbines are generating plenty of electricity, Landsvirkjun can ease off hydropower and leave more water in its reservoirs. When the wind drops, hydropower can pick up more of the demand.

That gives the utility more control over when it uses its stored water and helps that water go further.

In a recent development, german wind turbine maker Enercon manufactured Vaðölduver’s turbines. The project also includes a service and maintenance agreement with Enercon.

According to recent reports, landsvirkjun had a decade of experience operating pilot wind turbines before building Vaðölduver. One big thing they learned: They didn’t need tall towers to find plenty of wind.

It has been revealed that there’s little vegetation or other surface obstructions across this unique, exposed landscape. That allows the turbines to capture productive winds closer to the ground than they could at a more wooded or sheltered location.

“Lower” is relative, of course. The turbines still reach 150 meters (492 feet) at their highest blade tip.

The wind farm covers 17.1 square kilometers (6.6 square miles). Twenty-five turbines are rated at 4.26 MW each, and the remaining three at 4.5 MW. Landsvirkjun’s presentation puts annual generation at 440 GWh and lists a P50 net efficiency figure of 43%, which is considered strong for onshore wind.

The ability to tap into existing infrastructure was a major factor in Landsvirkjun’s site selection. Where a wind farm goes affects its cost, its environmental footprint, and the people who live nearby.

Recent findings suggest that landsvirkjun also identifies active engagement with communities and other stakeholders as essential to building wind projects. At Vaðölduver, the immediate task is to finish the remaining 14 turbines while the first phase completes its trial runs.

According to recent reports, the firm sees wind as a potential third pillar of Iceland’s electricity supply alongside hydropower and geothermal. Vaðölduver shows how those resources can work together, with wind adding generation while helping conserve stored water.

Iceland is a world leader in clean energy. It generates nearly 100% of its electricity from renewable sources, combining hydropower fueled by glacial runoff and rivers (around 70%) and geothermal energy (around 30%).

Over 90% of Icelandic households use direct geothermal hot water for space heating and hot water, while the remaining homes use renewable electricity.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s got the same grid capacity challenges as every other country. Adding wind – and anything else that uses power – means paying close attention to what the grid can handle. Iceland has an isolated transmission system, so maintaining stability and ensuring sufficient capacity are increasingly important as the country develops more projects.

While in Reykjavik, I met with the Minister of the Environment, Energy and Climate, Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, who told me that the Icelandic grid’s capacity is expected to grow from 20 TWh to 24-25 TWh within a decade. Jóhannsson also remarked that he is pro-data center and that investors are keen to establish more of them in the country.

Industry observers note that when I asked Jóhannsson and his team, as well as the teams at Landsvirkjun and publicly owned ON Power, Iceland’s second-largest electricity generator and largest EV charger network, about grid expansion looks to handle that pipeline, they all said that legislative reforms were being passed to speed up energy permitting processes. There is also financing in place to grow the grid. The physical transmission network is being expanded, but the process is slow because NIMBYism is creating bottlenecks.

In learning about latest and completed Icelandic power projects during my visit, it was apparent that the companies in the power and geothermal heat sector regularly collaborate on projects – everyone brings their expertise to the table and works for the common good (yes, really).

Industry observers note that but what was striking in discussions about grid expansion was that there seemed to be no looks to pitch in with the Icelandic transmission system operator (TSO), Landsnet hf. It seemed that the strategy was to let the TSO come up with the solutions on its own. At most, Jóhannsson’s team stated its legislative reform “opened the door” to possible grid innovations.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF YOU’RE JUST getting into golf, there will be a time in your life when you need to invest in a golf club set. As it’s a lifetime pursuit, it’s best to invest in a decent setup, and if well maintained, it can last you for years to come. While advanced players may want to customize their own golf club sets, there are numerous brands that make complete sets that will have you playing from day one. Even notable brands like Callaway and Wilson have solid options.

According to recent reports, it's true you could go buy pre-owned clubs as your first beginner set, which is not a bad idea to peruse your local Dick's Sporting Goods or local golf shop (especially for previous year model demos during the offseason), brand sites' used portals like Callaway Certified Pre-Owned, or eBay. But if you've gotten the golf bug and are looking for a newly introduced-to-you set, these days golf brands are churning out shiny, high-quality sets at affordable entry points. Customization is also better than ever, as several outfitters offer club length adjustments, different club combinations, and a selection of stylish golf bags to accompany them. You can always ask for a set as a great golf gift, too.

Whichever route you choose, we spoke with Paul Silva, head pro at NYC’s Van Cortlandt Golf Club to answer some of the most frequently asked questions when it comes to buying a beginner golf set. After you get a legit set, don't forget about some golf shoes.

When it comes to the game of golf, not many brands can boast expertise in every single category. One that can though is Callaway. The brand behind elite golf balls, top-tier putters, golf bags, pro-worthy irons and drivers, Callaway is no slouch when it comes to making high-quality gear for beginners.

It has been revealed that the 2026 XR lineup comes in a 13-piece set, which includes a mallet putter made by Odyssey and its DFX V-line Fang shape, which offers higher stability and more aggressive alignment aids—two elements you’re rarely going to find in an entry-level putter. The irons are classics, based on decades of stellar game-improvement technology, while the hybrids, 3-wood, and driver are modeled after one of golf’s most exciting new weapons of the past couple of years, the Paradym. This year you also get an approach wedge. Add on the fact of its high-MOI V-Line putter and you get a set that dominates the short game. This set will set you back more than most, but don’t be surprised if you tote these clubs along with you for the next ten years.Read More: The Best Golf Shirts.

Though technically a slightly older legacy bundle, this platinum set features two premium features we love. The first is the irons. They're well-built and just what you want out of a beginner iron, making them a solid set to build the base of your arsenal for years to come. Considered a game improvement set, they have a thinner top line and are more refined. The second is the golf bag: It's highly comfortable thanks to the dual carrying strap and lightweight design, and comes with ample pocket space.

Wilson is a brand with immense golf pedigree—no player worth their salt will scoff at the brand’s gear, whether you’re shooting even par or 20-over. The set is immensely affordable, so while it will probably long outlast your golf career, it won’t make you feel bad about upgrading once you start to improve.

Read More: Best Golf Clubs on Amazon.

For someone just getting into the game or hitting the range for the very first time, this set is great to start with. With every club you’ll need to get from the tee box to the green (and probably everywhere in between), this set won’t leave you without an option, no matter how wayward your shots get.

Sources indicate that the set has a solid 4.3-out-of-5-star rating on Amazon, with reviewers lauding the set’s value and high level of forgiveness. Odds are high you’ll want to upgrade sooner than later, but if you or someone you know likes to pick up new hobbies, this set will help decide if golf is a lifelong commitment or just a phase.

While one of the most expensive of the bunch, this TaylorMade set is certifiably legit. We're talking about a beast of a driver which features an adjustable driver, allowing you to change the loft and face angle as your swing evolves (something you hardly ever find on a complete set driver), a beautiful set of high-performance irons, and a stylish golf bag that will protect your investment with reassurance.

This is a set for those who are getting serious and playing several times per week. The barrier to entry is higher than the rest of the options on our list, but when you consider the pedigree of a brand like TaylorMade, you’ll find that the long lifespan of the clubs and golf bag make it a set you can grow into and not have to replace for years.

It has been revealed that picking up on the game quicker than you thought? You can skip the early stages and go for a complete set that allows you to learn how to optimize your shot-making skills. The Stix Perform Set is a complete 12-club set that will provide you with all the tools you need, all for under $1,000.

According to recent reports, the Perform Set is the brand’s first set with the option for irons with a steel shaft, a boon for mid-high handicap players whose higher swing speeds may be a bit too much for the extra flex of graphite. Clubs that benefit from the flex (the driver, 3 wood, and 4 hybrid) still come standard with graphite, but having the choice when selecting irons is going to greatly increase the amount of time you’ll stick with your Stix.

In my testing, I took the Stix out for a couple dozen rounds, walking and riding in a cart. The set is very manageable size-wise. The bag is light enough for comfortable wear but significant enough to stay secure when strapped to the back of a golf cart. They’re some of the most forgiving clubs I've played and are well-built, resulting in improved distance and fewer mishits. My favorite club was the 4 iron hybrid—I've never hit a hybrid so well.

Another set from one of the most prestigious equipment brands in golf, the Cobra Fly XL set is the ideal set for someone who knows they’re going to be consistently hitting the golf course in a golf cart. The cart bag is substantial, sturdy, and spacious, while the wide range of clubs gives you options in every part of the course.

The Cobra brand is well-recognized, and these striking clubs will fit in with any other sets on the course, ensuring that your skills do the talking, not your equipment. If your skills are lacking, that’s okay, too, because each club in this set is super forgiving thanks to excellent weight distribution and optimized shape, from the driver right down through the putter.

When you’re looking for a little more performance but still trying to stay affordable, PXG is a brand to look to. This Wildcat Bundle is an extremely versatile setup that utilizes premium materials and the same tech found in the brand’s standalone clubs, all tuned for maximum forgiveness and easy launch—must-haves for beginners.

Sources indicate that while it is a hefty investment, they’re the one-and-done purchase type, meaning that you won’t outgrow them anytime soon, and will last for years to come. These clubs are meant to bridge the gap from significant box store generic clubs and a custom-fitted pro set, while providing a fairway-friendly driver and the brand’s polymer cores for a softer feel and more distance. While it’s only a 9-club set, it has all the essentials you’ll need to make it up and down on any course.

Most beginner sets will include between nine and 11 clubs. 10 is a good sweet spot; it is enough to have a driver, a fairway wood and/or a hybrid, a 5i-9i, a wedge, and a putter. Generally a full set is 14 clubs; that includes the putter—and you can keep no more than that number in your bag during play.

According to recent reports, two recommendations we would make would be to forego a 3-wood in favor of a 5-wood or 4-hybrid—most players don’t actually need a 3-wood and would be better served with a more forgiving hybrid (or two). If you can, consider adding a sand wedge (or potentially a lob wedge that you learn how to use) to sit alongside your pitching wedge, as many pitching wedges aren’t lofted enough for tricky shots in the sand or around the greens.

As Silva told us, "I tell everyone the same thing in the beginning, find a few clubs that you can hit—a hybrid, a 5 iron, a 7 iron, a pitching wedge, a putter. You can learn to do a lot with those things, especially in the beginning. You don’t need to worry so much about distance.".

Most beginners will want a shaft made of graphite. These will create greater swing speeds, allowing you to hit the ball further, even as you start to tune your swing. If you’re not a full-on beginner or aren’t looking for any extra distance, a set with steel shafts are a great choice. These will be easier to grow into skill-wise, making it easier to adapt as your game improves. As your swing speed improves, the flex of graphite shafts will be too much, and you’ll need to graduate to iron shafts then.

Industry observers note that the main factors in forgiveness are club head and shaft. There’s a lot to dig into with this (we could write an entire essay on these two things), but in general, most beginner sets are outfitted with the absolute easiest club head to hit and a graphite shaft that allows for greater swing speed and fewer mistakes. We’d say not to get caught up in the nitty-gritty and focus on finding a set that is made for new players—something that almost every brand will outline in its product descriptions. Make sure you take a look to see what handicap each club set is designed for and pick the one made for high handicappers (that’s you), as these are coined as player improvement clubs.

Industry observers note that golf club prices run the gamut, but a good set of beginner clubs will usually run you anywhere from $250 to $1,000. This is a huge discrepancy, but there is a big range in quality from bottom to top. If you’re a brand-new golfer, spending $1,000 isn’t necessary, but if you think you’re in it for the long haul and want a set of sticks that are going to allow you to progress without having to upgrade, spending a little more cash is a great idea—the technology really does make a difference and it'll save you with an upgrade in a year or two if you improve.

Sources indicate that to help facilitate the best golf club sets on the market in 2026, I consulted with Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower (a mid-handicapper himself) to determine which clubs available are truly worthwhile. We evaluated each on club head size, materials, shaft construction, and forgiveness. Some sets, like the Stix full setup, gave us the chance to see what a quality set of clubs can do for a high handicapper, while the more affordable sets gave us a good idea of what is possible at a low price point. Even for someone like me, who may only get on the links a couple of times a year, using any of the sets listed below can have an instant improvement in gameplay. Brower typically plays around 20 rounds per year, so he definitely knows his way around a course. Ultimately, we picked sets that we liked the most, but there are so many options today, you really can’t go wrong when you’re trying to make a decision, because, hey, you can always upgrade.

In a recent development, beginners to golf do not need to get a custom fitting for clubs, but if you have the money and want to go all in on your new hobby, then we won't stop you. Really the main measurement you want to get right when buying is proper club sizing (not too tall or too short)—and the good news is most of these clubs will have a solid fit for just starting out.

Recent findings suggest that the only initial adjustments you need to make as a beginner are if you are exceptionally tall or short. If you are over 6'2" consider sizing a half-inch or more length adjustment on your clubs. You can also just opt for a set that has a "Tall" option available. If you are under 5'5", you'll likely want a half-inch decrease in length adjustment.

If you like to go by feel, swinging your friends’ clubs or talking to a pro at your local course will help confirm the sizing you need. As you progress in your game, sizing can be pinpointed down further to personalized club sizing, if you choose.

It has been revealed that there's nothing wrong with buying pre-owned clubs to serve as your first beginner set. There is a whole market online for really nice pre-owned clubs for a solid price on sites like Ebay and the golf brands' websites. Yet the downside is, you guessed it, they were somebody else's. There's wear and tear on them.

Industry observers note that instead of buying pre-owned, opt for fresh. A new set will give you the proper tools to get acclimated on the course and really give you the opportunity to learn the game. Golf is a lot about feel. Your clubs should be your best friend out on the course, not some raggedy set whose best days are long gone.

Buying a fresh set also gives you something to build off of. As you get better you'll want to make upgrades. Maybe you want a more precise sand wedge or a driver with more power? What you'll do next is swap out single clubs one at a time until you find a set that fits your game to a T.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even Alaska’s bears are not immune from accidentally making things weird or getting a bit too close. Over the summer, rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska watched an odd interaction between two unnamed black bears (Ursus americanus) taking part in Anan Creek’s salmon run.

“Sometimes the bears at Anan share the creek… a little too closely,” the rangers write. “One bear is waiting his turn for a prime fishing spot, and the other is so focused on the fish he doesn’t mind his surroundings. Did the 1st bear make it weird by backing up, or did the 2nd bear make it weird by staying there?”.

For this bit of humor, the rangers awarded the unnamed bears with the 2026 You Made it Weird Award.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

The largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in the region. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.
  • The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.
  • Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”.

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Sources indicate that being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

Recent findings suggest that while MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

Latest diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder remarked.

In a recent development, “Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also vital to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as newly introduced evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”.

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:.

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

Sources indicate that “MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

Recent findings suggest that “For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:.

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

Recent findings suggest that MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”.

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include newly introduced MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

Industry observers note that if you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder stated.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is vital that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”.

Allder remarked that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

In a recent development, “A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

Old solar panels have silver and copper worth recovering. A new US recycling firm called Jupiter prepares to send metals recovered from retired solar panels and data center hardware to Korea Zinc’s refineries, including a $7.4 billion plant planned for Clarksville, Tennessee.

According to recent reports, jupiter joins US solar panel recycler Solarcycle and PedalPoint Recycling, Korea Zinc’s US recycling and metals business, into a single, fully integrated organization. Jupiter says it’s launching with eight certified US facilities, nearly 1 million square feet of processing space, and about 250 employees. It’s also taking on customers from both businesses, including Microsoft, Prologis, and Brookfield.

For a solar farm or data center operator, that means a single tech giant can take equipment out of service, resell parts with remaining useful life, and recycle the rest. Customers can track where the materials go and bring them back into their own supply chains.

Korea Zinc will hold a majority stake. Solarcycle’s Suvi Sharma will lead Jupiter as CEO, and PedalPoint’s Kevin Hahm will be CFO. Microsoft and Prologis Ventures are among Solarcycle’s existing investors.

In a recent development, as Electrek reported in January, Solarcycle’s Cedartown, Georgia, plant was processing thousands of old solar panels a week when it opened. Solarcycle mentioned the plant could handle up to 5 gigawatts’ worth of panels annually at full capacity, recovering materials such as glass, aluminum, copper, and silver.

According to recent reports, the Tennessee plant adds a US refining step. Korea Zinc is developing the facility, called Project Crucible, with US government backing. It expects to start production in phases in 2029. The plant is designed to process about 1.1 million tons of raw materials per year and produce roughly 540,000 tons of finished products.

Tech Report: Hackers use old Bitly links to re-direct to offensive content

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media.
  • That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.
  • Link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media. According to the service provider Bitly, its hyperlinks in older tweets from many companies, politicians, and even government accounts are now redirecting to “content unrelated to the original posts.”.

That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.

Link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds. The service typically works by pinning a website’s lengthy, complex URL address to a tidied-up, abbreviated shortcut in a digital registry. This shortened address then redirects anyone who clicks it to their intended online destination.

Well…in theory. Security analysts have tried to warn people about an matter known as “bit rot” for decades. In 2009—about one year after Bitly’s debut—Silicon Valley entrepreneur Joshua Schacter wrote a prescient blog post cautioning against what he felt were potentially serious flaws in the link-shortening “middleman” system. Amid the concerns, Schacter cited a “latest and potentially unreliable” tool that ties an original hyperlink to the “health of a third party.”.

Industry observers note that “The shortener may decide a link is a Terms Of Service violation and delete it. If the shortener accidentally erases a database, forgets to renew its domain, or just disappears, the link will break,” he explained. “If a top-level domain changes its policy on commercial use, the link will break. If the shortener gets hacked, every link becomes a potential phishing attack.”.

Industry observers note that it now appears bad actors recently identified countless of these Bitly links previously posted across social media between 2009 and 2014. Although their exact methods aren’t clear, it’s possible they generated their own custom Bitly links using the addresses in the social media posts, then used those to send people to different destinations. Bitly notes its links do not automatically expire, but paid customers may redirect existing links.

In a recent development, many examples were found among the more than 60,000 posts on X from President Donald Trump’s official account. In one of Trump’s previous posts about his golf course in Scotland, the Bitly link temporarily redirected to Wikipedia’s entry on the Epstein Files. Targets also included corporations like McDonald’s, with one of the fast food giant’s 2011 Bitly URLs suddenly linked to Wikipedia’s page about the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

Sources indicate that not every hijacked post funneled people to upsetting outcomes. Instead of a cybersecurity PSA, the Bitly address in a 2021 post from the FBI briefly linked to a photo of a blubbery seal. Another of Trump’s URLs sent you to the popular video game, Geometry Dash.

In its acknowledgement of the problem on November 15, Bitly reported it had identified and suspended the bad actors’ accounts, and were in the process of “disabling the affected links.”.

“Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the concern and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future,” Bitly wrote at the time.

What Is the Difference Between a Comforter and a Duvet Insert?

A comforter is a single, often quilted, piece of bedding with a fabric cover encasing the doughy fill in between the two fabric layers. A duvet, on the other hand, refers to both the insert and fabric cover. A comforter can be colorful or white, and made in a variety of fabrics. The fabric cover of a comforter is stitched directly onto the fill (down, feathers, or polyester are most common). A duvet’s cover is removable, and often tied to the corners via loops attached to the insert.

According to recent reports, not necessarily. Many duvet inserts are designed to be used on their own, as a comforter, or with a cover. I recommend a cover to help protect your duvet insert, ensure it lasts as long as possible, and make laundry day as easy as possible. Duvet covers act as a protective layer, keeping sweat, body oils, and normal wear from affecting your duvet insert. Plus, duvet covers allow you to add personality to your bedscape, whether you prefer an all-white minimalist look or a maximalist ruffle.

What Is the Best Type of Filling for a Duvet?

Sources indicate that similar to quality, the “best” filling is pretty subjective. People often choose silk, lyocell, down, or down-alternative fills. Down comforters tend to be firmer and heavier, while down-alternatives are usually considered more lightweight and airy. Down-alternatives derive from recycled and allergen-friendly materials, so they’re ideal for people who prefer or require those types of fillings. The fill power will also determine the ultimate comfort level, and most should hover around 650 for a down, cotton candy-like feel.

In a recent development, and again, those care instructions come into play. If you’d rather throw your comforter in the wash, that’s most down comforters in our list can handle it. Meanwhile, some specialty down-alternatives (like bamboo viscose options) need to take a trip to the dry cleaners, which can make them higher maintenance and more expensive long-term.

Does the Quality of a Duvet Insert Matter?

In terms of “quality,” you’ll see the effects in two main areas: the price point and longevity of your duvet insert. For instance, a down comforter with 750 fill power like Brooklinen’s heavyweight comforter is specifically designed for keeping you warm during colder winter months (or for anyone who spends most nights shivering). The fill power makes it lofty and fluffy, but the construction can also keep it lofty and fluffy.

According to recent reports, baffle-box construction, as mentioned above, is also considered a higher quality design option, which holds fill in separate chambers to keep the fill even. All of this remarked, the most expensive, technically high-quality comforters aren’t necessarily the best for every type of sleeper. And while we love comforters and duvet inserts that run as high as $500, we’ve also scoured the internet and tested alternatives you can shop for less than $100 on Amazon (we’re looking at you, Bedsure Waffle Comforter Set).

It’s also important to keep in mind that your duvet insert’s quality depends on how you care for it. Make sure to carefully read the care instructions, and if needed, take it to a trustworthy dry cleaner for a gentle clean (experts say about two to three times per year).

How Do You Put a Duvet Cover on an Insert or Comforter?

Follow these steps from Monelle Totah, cofounder of Hudson Grace, for a lump-free way to put an insert or comforter inside a duvet cover:.

How Do I Wash a Duvet Insert/Comforter?

It has been revealed that it’s notable to always check your specific product’s care instructions before washing. For example, the Buffy Breeze duvet insert recommends a spot clean or dry clean only, while the Boll & Branch comforter is machine washable on a gentle cycle. To take out the guesswork, we’ve included the product’s care instructions right above each of our review descriptions.

Diana Ciechorska, general manager at Park Slope Cleaning, a commercial cleaning company in Fresh York City, claims the standard first step for washing your comforter includes treating any visible stains before you load the comforter into the washing machine. “Opt for a gentle cycle with cold water, using a mild detergent,” she says. “An extra rinse cycle ensures no detergent residue remains.”.

In a recent development, when taking a comforter out of the dryer, Parima Ijaz, the New Jersey–based founder of bedding line Pure Parima, recommends holding the corners to shake and fluff it. This allows the fill to distribute even after being jumbled up in the dryer. If possible, she states it’s ideal to let the comforter air-dry for an extra day to make sure it is completely dry before dressing your bed.

How Often Should You Wash Your Comforter?

Comforters and duvet inserts accumulate “dust, sweat, and oils, which can cause allergies and wear down the fabric,” states Camden Olivero, COO and cofounder of Clotheslyne, an on-demand pick-up and delivery laundry service. With this in mind, I recommend washing your comforter two to three times a year to help keep allergens at bay and the covering in its best condition (double check the label first, though).

How Should You Store a Comforter?

Like your other linens, it’s best to keep your comforter in a cool, dry place to avoid mold or moisture buildup. Keep the comforter out of plastic and cedar too, as these materials can cause yellowing.

How Do You Dispose of Old Comforters?

According to recent reports, if your old comforter is still in good condition, we recommend donating it to charities in your area. However, if you’re looking to purely dispose of old comforters, organizations like Trashie ethically recycle textiles for you to keep them out of landfills—so long as they’re clean and free of soil like motor oil or paint.

What Kind of Duvet Inserts Do Hotels Use?

If you want to mimic your latest hotel stay at home, you’re not alone. We’ve reviewed the best hotel comforters, which are often sold on luxury hotel chain websites like Marriott and Four Seasons. There are several getaways that use Frette’s bedding, too, including The Palace Hotel in Madrid. In most hotel duvet inserts, there are a few common traits: decadent down or hypoallergenic, plant-based down-alternative fills; high fill powers, around 800; organic cotton or bamboo viscose covers for breathability; and carefully designed baffle-box or box-stitch construction to keep fill in place and make it last.

Are Duvet Inserts Machine Washable?

Fortunately, most of our favorite duvet inserts are machine washable and can even go in the dryer. Some will require a commercial washer (especially if they’re bulky), though, and others like the comforters from Quince and Cozy Earth should take a trip to the dry cleaners. Read the care label, and see what’s best for your duvet insert.

Ijaz recommends washing your comforter in a front-loading washing machine since an upright machine is too abrasive. “Using a top loader with a spindle in the middle can damage the comforter and make it harder to properly and evenly wash it,” she says. Otherwise, her general suggestions are like what the experts noted in this story: Wash your comforter on a cold, gentle cycle and avoid harsh softeners and chemicals so the shell and fill stay in the best condition.

How Do I Choose the Right Duvet Insert for Different Seasons?

There are duvet inserts and comforters with heavy fill powers (think 800 and above) for harsh winter months or cold sleepers, lightweight options (400 or below) for summer months or hot sleepers, and medium weights (around 400 to 600) for year-round comfort. We’ve also learned that the fluffiest duvet inserts often give sleepers that Goldilocks-level sleep. “A fluffy, high-loft duvet delivers the most consistent sleep experience across seasons,” Anthony Loiacono, director of rooms at L’Auberge de Sedona, previously told AD. “It provides warmth without weight, and most importantly, adapts to day-to-night temperature shifts.” Frette’s Cortina Medium Down Duvet Filler has all-season appeal, and you can always layer with an extra blanket if you want more coverage on colder nights.

According to recent reports, not all duvet inserts are created equal. This is a lesson you learn early on, when you wake up either sweating or freezing in the middle of the night. The fact is that this annoying experience is also completely avoidable. Reading up on the duvet insert you're considering buying—and actually understanding what all the terms mean—will tell you everything you need to know, including how hot it’s going to be and whether or not the down is going to end up smooshed in one corner come morning. So, I put this guide together with the help of Danielle Trotter, the textiles technical designer at West Elm, to break down what to consider in the confusing world that is duvet insert fillings, fill power, and the different types of construction.

Recent findings suggest that fill Power: This is the measurement of how much down occupies a cubic inch of space in the insert, a.k.a. how “lofty” it feels. You’ll usually see numbers in the 500s and up. The higher the fill power, the fluffier and warmer it will feel. I typically like fill powers that hover around 800 during the colder months. This fill power is typically on the marshmallowy side of the spectrum and feels cozier and insulating when the temperature outside starts to drop. For the summertime, 600 fill power or so is usually a sweet spot for me since it’s more airy and breathable, but individual preferences may vary.

In a recent development, corner Loops: If there are corner loops or anchor loops, that means you can use the comforter as a duvet insert. If there are no loops, the comforter might be prone to clumping and bunching within the duvet, so we wouldn’t recommend it unless you have a lot of patience. Some of the loops in this list reach up to 12, which are super helpful to keep the fill even.

Fill Content: Fill material is usually classified as either down or down alternative options.

It has been revealed that outer Shell: The material on the outer shell of your comforter or duvet insert matters. Look at the thread count. I find that fabrics with thread counts around 300 are typically spongy and airy. Consider your preferred sleeping temperature and whether a cotton sateen shell that’s smooth but slightly thicker is a better option than one made of crisp percale cotton. If you’re a hot sleeper, you’ll probably want a cooling material with breathability, like eucalyptus.

Size and Color: The size of your insert is dictated by the size of your bed. Companies usually offer all standard sizes from twin to king, with some brands offering California king as well. In terms of color, white is most popular for the duvet insert, but you can also find ivory relatively easily. Comforter color ranges are more expansive, and you can likely find a hue that fits your decor. I’ve called out what’s available in each of the product picks.

Thread Count: This is the number of horizontal and vertical threads per square inch of the duvet insert's outer fabric. Expert tip: “In theory, people think that the higher the thread count, the better the quality because more yarns are being used,” Trotter indicates. “However, it’s the quality of the yarns or even the type of weave that really matters!”.

It has been revealed that baffle-Box Construction: This design means the comforter or duvet insert has sewn-in square chambers with side walls. “Each chamber has an equal amount of fill, and the side walls prevent the fill from shifting,” claims Trotter. “This construction is considered to be of a better quality because warmth is evenly distributed.”.

Sewn-Through Construction: This type of construction is when the duvet insert is made of two pieces of fabric sewn around the perimeter, then filled and quilted into squares. This means the top and bottom of the comforter are sewn together. In turn, the fill is shift- and bunch-resistant. While this is a great option for those who like low-maintenance laundry days since you can typically toss these comforter types in the washing machine, the tighter construction usually makes the fill less lofty. Plus, cold air can seep through the seams, so it’s more ideal for a summer bedscape.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, around the world, the number of uncontacted Indigenous tribes continues to dwindle. Indigenous rights advocates estimate that half of the nearly 200 communities still existing in comparative isolation could disappear within a decade, without proper safeguards against climate change, land loss, fame-seeking opportunists, and illegal industrial encroachments. Unfortunately, the situation has apparently grown so dire that some Indigenous groups are reaching out for help—and exposing themselves to potentially deadly foreign diseases in the process.

Sources indicate that on November 17, the nonprofit advocacy group Survival International reported a recent incident in which 20 members of the Awá people intentionally contacted local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon. Although proficient hunter-gatherers, the group requested yams before taking them back into the rainforest.

“This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International director Caroline Pearce noted in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that the Awá are one of the world’s last uncontacted Indigenous tribes, whose ties to the Brazilian rainforest stretch back centuries. They faced their first attacks from European settlers during the 1800s, which eventually forced them to adopt a nomadic lifestyle to avoid future encounters. Brazil finally supplied the Awá with settlement areas during the mid-1980s, but it still took years before the government properly invested in demarcated land. In the meantime, numerous deadly interactions with loggers, farmers, and other illegal intruders had reduced the Awá community to barely 300 people. Of those, advocates estimate only about one-third of the hunter-gatherers remain completely isolated from the outside world.

“The Brazilian government must commit the resources necessary to protect [the region of] Arariboia from the loggers and ranchers who are razing it, in flagrant defiance of the law,” Pearce added.

Industry observers note that in addition to the advocacy work by Survival International, the Awá are supported by a team of Indigenous members of the Guajajara community known as the Forest Guardians. These volunteers have spent years pushing back against illegal cattle ranchers and loggers attempting to claim land in Arariboia, often dying as a result of their efforts.

“The Forest Guardians have always worked to protect the Awá against encroachment, even at the cost of losing warriors in battle,” the organization mentioned. “We demand immediate action from the relevant authorities…to ensure what the Awá believe is best for them, safeguarding their lives, health, safety and dignity. FOR THE AWÁ, FOR THE TENETEHAR [language], AND FOR THE FOREST!”.

What Is the Best Type of Yogurt? We Narrowed It Down to the World’s 8 Healthiest.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that EVERYBODY LOVE YOGURT.
  • Recent findings suggest that "Most of the world is lactose intolerant and has been for thousands and thousands of years," says Robert Hutkins, PhD, a professor of food microbiology at the University of Nebraska.
  • Whether you need help digesting lactose or not, the latest research suggests that yogurt has wide-ranging benefits, from enhancing gut health to improving blood sugar control to maybe even reducing your risk of an early death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that EVERYBODY LOVE YOGURT. Okay, maybe not everyone, but there's a reason yogurt has been a dietary staple in dozens of countries for centuries. Yogurt doesn't spoil as fast as milk, yet still delivers milk's nutrients—protein, calcium, potassium, magnesium—without the same risk of, um, certain GI concerns.

Recent findings suggest that "Most of the world is lactose intolerant and has been for thousands and thousands of years," says Robert Hutkins, PhD, a professor of food microbiology at the University of Nebraska. "Humans figured out that even if they were lactose intolerant, they could still consume cultured milks because the culture helps degrade the lactose before it gets to the colon and gets fermented by gas-producing microbes.".

Whether you need help digesting lactose or not, the latest research suggests that yogurt has wide-ranging benefits, from enhancing gut health to improving blood sugar control to maybe even reducing your risk of an early death.

According to recent reports, from Europe to Asia to Africa, all yogurt starts with the same basic ingredients: milk and good bacteria. But no two types are exactly alike. Here's what to know before your next grocery run.

Recent findings suggest that traditional Greek yogurt is strained through a cheesecloth to remove excess fluid. Yogurt factories use centrifuges or special filters instead. What's left behind is a thick, smooth yogurt with a slightly acidic flavor and a concentrated source of nutrients, including about 18 grams of protein per 6-ounce container.

Some food makers add thickeners as a shortcut, so check the label for a simple ingredient list of milk, cream, and yogurt cultures. "The products with thickeners added have a different texture, a little bit more gumminess," says Molly Kimball, RD, CSSD, a dietitian based in Louisiana. Swap in Greek yogurt for sour cream or mayo, or stir it into guacamole—the lactic acid slows down the oxidation that turns avocados brown.

Technically considered a soft cheese, skyr is strained like Greek yogurt to produce something firm yet creamy. It's usually made with skim milk, yielding yogurt with slightly more protein than Greek yogurt: about 19 grams of protein per 6 ounces. Use skyr to make dips hearty enough to stand up to cut vegetables (or chips). Or stir it into bolognese to impart a velvety texture and an extra boost of protein.

This yogurt variety isn't strained, so it has a thinner texture and less protein than its Greek or Icelandic cousins: about 6 grams per 6 ounces. Traditional Bulgarian yogurt gets its signature sharp flavor from high concentrations of the aptly named Lactobacillus Bulgaricus bacteria, which produce lactic acid. Kimball recommends blending Bulgarian yogurt into smoothies to add a tanginess that counterbalances sweeter ingredients.

Recent findings suggest that most yogurts are fermented in large vats. As yogurt bacteria digest milk, they produce a wide variety of metabolites, including gel-like substances called exopolysaccharides. Then the yogurt is pumped into the smaller containers we snag at the grocery store.

With French-style yogurt, the milk and bacterial cultures are poured into cups earlier, before the microbes multiply. "That gives you a more custardy product because it hasn't gone through this pumping phase that disturbs the gel," says Hutkins. Inside a 6-ounce cup of French-style yogurt, you'll find about 5 grams of protein. To try it the French way, eat your yogurt for dessert, alone or paired with a little honey or jam.

Industry observers note that this tangy, thin, pourable yogurt is fermented with kefir grains–gelatinous clusters that contain milk proteins and up to 50 bacterial and yeast species. During fermentation, these yeasts can leave behind traces of alcohol and carbon dioxide, or fizz. However, many mass-produced kefirs use standardized starter cultures instead to maintain consistent product quality and keep the alcohol concentration low enough to sell in grocery stores.

In a recent development, kimball suggests drinking plain kefir, Russian or otherwise. It packs about 8 grams of protein per cup. If you can't handle the sour flavor, balance it with a teaspoon or less of maple syrup or a few drops of stevia or monk fruit. If you want a flavored variety, pick one with no more than 5 grams of added sugar.

Sweet and mildly acidic, dahi is the key ingredient in Indian staples like lassi–a yogurt drink often flavored with mango, spices, or rosewater–and raita, the sauce that cools your mouth when you order your vindaloo extra hot. Some dahi varieties contain Leuconostoc, bacteria that produce a metabolite called diacetyl that imparts a buttery flavor. Each six-ounce serving of dahi packs about 7 grams of protein.

Drinkable like kefir, laban is sour but smooth and contains about 5 grams of protein per six ounces. Strain it in a colander or cheesecloth to make labneh, a thick, soft, yogurt-like cheese traditionally smeared on sandwiches and stacked on mezze platters.

This drinkable yogurt is often thicker than fermented milk beverages. Its mix of cultures, which hail mostly from the Lactobacillusgenus, imparts a moderately acidic flavor with subtle buttery notes. Amasi packs about 6 grams of protein per six ounces. It's traditionally eaten with maize or sorghum porridge, especially at breakfast.

#133001. Tech Report: RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1009 w)

Tech Report: RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F.
  • Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.
  • A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

Recent findings suggest that in December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” mentioned Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

Recent findings suggest that “The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”.

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

Industry observers note that however, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the latest approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse noted.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”.

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse remarked the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse noted.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”.

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

In a recent development, “There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.
