  • Sources indicate that officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone.
  • Recent findings suggest that the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Sources indicate that officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

Recent findings suggest that the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with new tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

Industry observers note that the sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han states he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

Recent findings suggest that “I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student remarked in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

It has been revealed that in the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place new anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin swiftly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never said he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

While fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be upcoming concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an important role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

#132954. I Went to Gee’s Bend to See Its Famous Quilts. Nothing Prepared Me for the Beauty

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1208 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

I Went to Gee’s Bend to See Its Famous Quilts. Nothing Prepared Me for the Beauty

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line.
  • I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares.
  • Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line. Over my shoulder, Doris Pettway Mosely watches my hands with the patience of someone who has been quilting since she was 11. She gently corrects my angle and sewing style, while Mary Margaret Pettway does the same for the rest of our small class. We laugh through most of it. Then Doris looks over my work and tells me my stitches are nice and short, and I sit up a little straighter.

I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares. Mary Margaret, a fourth-generation quilter, has shown her work in major museums across the country. Doris, the daughter of celebrated quilter Leola Pettway, still sews her mother’s signature Z pattern alongside her own vivid, scrap-pieced designs. “I learned at four years old,” Mary Margaret tells me, explaining that she picked up the craft from her mother, Lucy T. Pettway. In their house, quilting was a chore like mopping or sweeping the yard, and the boys learned too.

Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.

Industry observers note that after class, I wander the festival grounds, where quilts hang from clotheslines strung between wooden posts. A quilt of nested squares in navy and sky blue hangs next to one in butter yellow, punched with blocks of chartreuse and red. Another glows neon coral. Farther down the line, rings of pale pink, olive green, and rose-print fabric radiate out from a single center square, a take on the classic Housetop pattern. Inside the River Gallery, a quilt called Remembering Dinah is pieced from faded denim and mustard corduroy, its back pockets and frayed knees left intact. It’s a reminder of where this tradition began.

Children learning to quilt in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, in 2010.

Today, Gee’s Bend quilts hang in more than 40 museums, but they began as something far more practical. This small town takes its name from Joseph Gee, who established a cotton plantation in this bend of the Alabama River in 1816. Enslaved people and generations of their descendants stitched quilts to keep their families warm during winter and to brighten their homes, piecing them together from worn-out work clothes, denim, and whatever fabric scraps they had. Each year as summer gave way to fall, women hung their quilts outside to air before the cold set in, a tradition that inspired the Airing of the Quilts Festival, debuted in 2022 by nonprofit organizations Freedom Quilting Bee Legacy and Sew Gee’s Bend Heritage Builders.

A quilt on display in Gee’s Bend, Alabama.

Recent findings suggest that among the community’s earliest known named quilters was Dinah Miller, who was taken from West Africa as a girl in 1860, likely aboard the Clotilda, the last known slave ship to reach the US. She settled in Gee’s Bend in the 1890s and passed her craft down. During the civil rights movement, the quilts became a financial lifeline. Black residents who tried to register to vote risked losing their jobs and the land they lived on to white landowners. In 1962, officials shut down the ferry connecting the community to the county seat, making it difficult to register to vote, and cutting them off from grocery stores, banks, schools, and medical care. The ferry didn’t run again until 2006.

Sources indicate that four years after the closure, the community established the Freedom Quilting Bee, a cooperative that gave local women an income their white employers couldn’t take away. When Father Francis X. Walter, an Episcopal priest and Mobile native, saw the bold quilts on a trip to Wilcox County, he helped organize auctions in Upcoming York, where the striking designs caught the attention of tastemakers like Sister Parish. The quilts went on to sell at Bloomingdale’s and Saks Fifth Avenue.

“The Quilts of Gee's Bend” exhibit at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, in 2004.

In a recent development, the art world caught up decades later, when a landmark exhibition, “The Quilts of Gee’s Bend,” opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, in 2002, introducing the quilters to audiences far beyond Alabama. Today, their work is celebrated for its bold colors, inventive patterns, and astonishing craftsmanship. In 2006, 10 of the quilts appeared on US postage stamps. And this summer, Ralph Lauren released a limited-edition collection of apparel, quilts, and home goods featuring designs by quilters Claudia Pettway Charley and Loretta Pettway Bennett.

But for design lovers, the festival offers something no museum can: the chance to see the quilts in the place they were made, and to meet the individual women who made them. They’re still sewn by hand, too. “[An authentic] Gee’s Bend quilt is not quilted by a sewing machine,” Mary Margaret indicates. “And it’s notable to understand that every quilt is not alike. Everyone who quilts is not alike.”.

Our quilting class ends the way it began, with plenty of laughter as we tie off our last stitches. Everyone wants a photo with Doris and Mary Margaret, and a few students have even brought books featuring the quilters’ work to be signed.

Outside, the festival is in full swing, with more than 40 booths devoted to quilters selling their quilts and wall hangings, along with puzzles and notebooks printed with Gee’s Bend patterns, doormats, quilted totes, and pot holders.

According to recent reports, last year’s festival drew more than 2,500 people and over $870,000 in visitor spending for the state, and Mary Margaret indicates guests come from as far as France and England. “They want to immerse themselves in Gee’s Bend,” she says. Doris looks forward to it all year. “I get to meet a lot of people I’ve never seen before,” she says. This year, she was especially excited to meet a 97-year-old quilter from Marion, Alabama, whose work she admires.

Quilts hanging outside at the festival.

I’ve visited plenty of places where Black history is told in the past tense, on plaques and behind glass. Gee’s Bend feels different. Here, the history is alive, and the people who inherited it are setting the terms. That hasn’t always been easy. Over the years, says Mary Margaret, quilters have seen their work copied and sold without receiving compensation. The festival allows the public to buy directly from the quilters, at their booths or even from their porches, and know that the money is going straight to the artists.

Mostly, my day with the women of Gee’s Bend feels like a family reunion. The experience takes me straight back to childhood afternoons with my grandmother, who taught me to mend holes in pockets, sew patches onto my jeans jacket, and replace a button before anyone noticed it was missing.

Industry observers note that mary Margaret started even younger than I did, and now her own son and daughter are quilters themselves, working with patterns passed down through generations of the family. “To me a quilt indicates home,” says Mary Margaret. “It says warmth. It says care. It says time.”.

Latest Update: What Is Self-Custody? How to Hold Your Own Crypto Keys

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when you buy crypto on an exchange, the exchange usually holds it for you.
  • The risk is that if an exchange collapses, is hacked or freezes withdrawals, its customers can lose access to their funds.
  • You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when you buy crypto on an exchange, the exchange usually holds it for you. Your account demonstrates a balance, but the private keys that control the coins belong to the trading platform.

The risk is that if an exchange collapses, is hacked or freezes withdrawals, its customers can lose access to their funds. The collapse of FTX in November 2022 left millions of users unable to withdraw, and turned the old crypto saying "not your keys, not your coins" into a rallying cry.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

It has been revealed that self-custody is the alternative: holding your crypto yourself, with no intermediary standing between you and your money. This guide explains what self-custody is, how it works, the tools available and the risks it brings.

Self-custody means you, and only you, control the private keys to your crypto.

On a blockchain, coins are not stored in a wallet in the way cash sits in a purse. They are recorded on a public ledger, and a private key, a long secret number, is what proves you have the right to spend them. Whoever holds the private key controls the coins.

In a recent development, with a custodial service, such as a centralized exchange, the firm holds the keys on your behalf, and you rely on it to process your withdrawals. With a self-custodial, or non-custodial, wallet, the keys are generated and stored on your own device, and transactions only happen when you approve them.

When you set up a self-custodial wallet, it generates a seed phrase, usually a list of 12 or 24 words. The seed phrase is a human-readable backup of your private keys: anyone who has it can recreate your wallet on another device and move your funds.

Recent findings suggest that that makes the seed phrase the single most notable thing to protect. Most guides recommend writing it down on paper or stamping it into metal, storing it somewhere safe offline, and never typing it into a website, sharing it or saving it in a photo or cloud file.

Self-custodial wallets come in several forms:.

Sources indicate that custodial services are easier to use. If you forget your password, you can reset it, and an exchange handles the security of its own systems. But you are trusting the organization to stay solvent, keep your funds safe and let you withdraw when you want to.

Self-custody removes that counterparty risk, and means no tech giant can freeze your funds or block a transaction. The tradeoff is responsibility: there is no password reset. If you lose your seed phrase, or someone steals it, there is usually no way to get your crypto back.

Welshman James Howells indicates the keys to about 8,000 BTC are on a hard drive that was thrown out in 2013 and buried in a landfill in Newport, Wales.

Losing your keys is the most common risk, but not the only one.

According to recent reports, hardware can have flaws. In July 2026, a firmware vulnerability in Coldcard, a Bitcoin-only air-gapped hardware wallet, let attackers reconstruct some customers' seed phrases. Losses rose to nearly $114 million in Bitcoin within days, according to Galaxy Research. Even the most secure devices depend on their makers getting the code right.

Phishing and malware are a constant threat to software wallets, and scammers often pose as wallet support staff to trick owners into handing over seed phrases.

Holders also face physical danger. So-called "wrench attacks," in which criminals use violence to force victims to hand over crypto, have surged. Blockchain security firm CertiK verified 52 wrench attacks worldwide in the first half of 2026, up from 39 a year earlier, and Chainalysis said such attacks were on pace for a record year.

The threat is one reason holders have pushed back against proposals to make them report large self-custody holdings to tax authorities, warning that such records could leak.

Moving crypto off an exchange generally involves a few steps:.

Regulators have long debated how to handle self-custodial, or "unhosted," wallets. In October 2026, the U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network withdrew a 2020 proposal that would have required banks and money services businesses to keep records on transactions with self-custodial wallets over $3,000 and report those over $10,000.

In France, the Senate rejected a proposal in November 2026 that would have required holders to declare self-custodied crypto worth more than €100,000.

Sources indicate that self-custody is starting to extend beyond humans. In 2026, MetaMask launched Agent Wallet, a self-custodial wallet that lets AI agents execute on-chain trades within limits set by the user, while Coinbase introduced its own self-custodial wallets for AI agents.

Recent findings suggest that wallet makers are also working to make self-custody easier for newcomers, with features such as social logins and passkeys that reduce reliance on seed phrases. But the core principle remains the same: whoever controls the keys controls the crypto.

Rivian’s upcoming electric bike spinoff, ALSO, has hit another speed bump. The organization has announced that it is temporarily halting deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycles after discovering software-related problems affecting some bikes, including issues with charging behavior.

In a recent development, and unfortunately, this isn’t entirely surprising. We’ve already reported on some strange battery behavior with the latest e-bikes, as well as customers having to send their bikes back for repairs.

In a message sent to customers, ALSO explained that it was pausing shipments to address several software problems before more bikes reach riders.

“We’ve identified a few software-based challenges, such as charging behavior, that are impacting some bikes,” the organization explained.

ALSO says its engineers are working on a firmware enhancement to resolve the problems, with shipments expected to resume in approximately two weeks.

The pause affects the remaining Launch Edition deliveries as well as the beginning of Performance Edition shipments, both of which will now arrive later than previously promised.

The announcement follows earlier reports of unusual charging and discharging behavior on the TM-B, which we previously highlighted as some of the growing pains facing Rivian’s ambitious new e-bike venture.

We’ve also reported on customers needing to return their bikes for repairs, raising questions about how smoothly the organization’s initial rollout was progressing.

The problems align with many of our initial concerns we discussed a year ago when the bike was first unveiled, namely that the high-tech design means the bike incorporates many new and proprietary systems that could each lead to complicated and costly failures.

Now ALSO has officially acknowledged software problems affecting some bikes, including charging behavior, though it hasn’t detailed the full extent of the issues or confirmed whether they are directly related to those earlier reports.

Recent findings suggest that I love the PR spin how only "some" bikes are affected. If it's the same bike running the same software, it's affected. The only bikes not affected are the ones that haven't been delivered, because they are not being used.

The bike represents a fairly radical departure from traditional electric bicycles, with proprietary technology throughout its drivetrain and control systems. That makes software an especially crucial part of the ownership experience.

Industry observers note that to ALSO’s credit, pausing deliveries to fix known problems is probably the right move. Nobody wants to receive a premium-priced electric bicycle only to discover that it needs an immediate trip back to the manufacturer.

But for customers who have already waited longer than expected, another delay is undoubtedly frustrating.

ALSO says it will provide another enhancement on November 24, hopefully with better news about when deliveries can resume.

According to recent reports, last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. Tesla toughens FSD driver monitoring in Europe while loosening it in the US

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is rolling out stricter driver monitoring for its “Full Self-Driving” system in Europe, with earlier warnings, a full strike for drivers who look away during a manoeuvre, and a hands-on-wheel requirement above 130 km/h (81 mph).
  • Industry observers note that in the US, Tesla has spent the last year going the other way.
  • Sources indicate that on November 16, the Dutch vehicle authority RDW unveiled that it signed off on a new enhancement to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for FSD (Supervised) in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is rolling out stricter driver monitoring for its “Full Self-Driving” system in Europe, with earlier warnings, a full strike for drivers who look away during a manoeuvre, and a hands-on-wheel requirement above 130 km/h (81 mph).

Industry observers note that in the US, Tesla has spent the last year going the other way. Its CEO told owners they can text and drive on FSD, and recent US builds were tuned to nag drivers less.

Sources indicate that on November 16, the Dutch vehicle authority RDW unveiled that it signed off on a new enhancement to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for FSD (Supervised) in Europe. It covers HW4 vehicles and goes out over the air.

Sources indicate that according to the RDW, drivers now get attention warnings earlier. If a driver isn’t paying attention while the system performs a manoeuvre, they get a “full strike.” The regulator notes the update also adds measures to prevent misuse of the system, but it didn’t spell out what they are.

There’s a speed component too. Above 130 km/h (where legal), the driver has to keep their hands on the wheel. And setting a maximum speed above what the system displays now requires the driver to confirm it by scrolling the wheel up, with the speed limit sign pulsing red when the car goes over.

The RDW says it tested the revision on its own track and on public roads and found no adverse or unintended effects. Ten other countries have adopted the Dutch approval so far, with Finland now on the list, while EU-wide approval is still waiting on a vote at the TCMV, the committee of member states.

This comes two weeks after Tesla cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe and dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name there. Germany had made both a condition of supporting EU approval.

Now look at how Tesla handles the same software at home.

Sources indicate that at Tesla’s shareholder meeting last November, Musk complained that the car was “a little strict about keeping your eyes on the road” and said Tesla would “allow you to text and drive essentially” within a month or two. A month later, an owner asked whether FSD v14.2.1 allowed texting. Musk’s answer: “Depending on context of surrounding traffic, yes.”.

Texting while driving is illegal in 49 states. FSD is still a Level 2 system, and Tesla’s own fine print says the driver is responsible at all times.

In May, Musk confirmed that FSD v14.3.3 was built to nag drivers less. Tesla did add better eye-gaze tracking and eyewear handling in a June build, to be fair. But the pitch to owners hasn’t changed: fewer nags is sold as a feature.

And US drivers have been allowed to go hands-free on FSD at any speed since Tesla moved to cabin-camera monitoring in 2024. There’s no 130 km/h rule here.

In a recent development, NHTSA noticed. In its engineering analysis of FSD crashes in low-visibility conditions, the agency asked Tesla to justify a list of its marketing claims, and it specifically cited Musk’s texting post. In September, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi asked NHTSA to look into Tesla’s driver monitoring after dozens of videos appeared to show drivers asleep on Autopilot and FSD.

Industry observers note that the results are on the road. Last month, a driver told the CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove through a freeway closure and hit a patrol car, seriously injuring two officers. Owners are also filming themselves defeating Tesla’s driver monitoring and posting it for clout.

Both markets get the same cabin camera and the same HW4 computer.

Industry observers note that but in Europe, a type-approval authority tests every update before it ships and can refuse it. In the US, nobody pre-approves driver-assist software. Tesla self-certifies, and NHTSA only steps in after complaints and crashes pile up, which is how you end up with a CEO publicly telling owners to text while the regulator is still writing letters about it.

This enhancement proves Tesla can build stricter driver monitoring whenever a regulator demands it. The code exists. It’s running on HW4 cars in 11 European countries right now.

Industry observers note that that's because Musk is buddies with the current federal government that would regulate his not-full-self-driving system. Whereas Europe doesn't kowtow to his whims. We'll see what happens in 2029 with a new administration.

That makes the US approach hard to defend. Tesla’s argument for relaxing supervision is that FSD is now good enough. But if that were true, it would be showing the RDW data proving looser monitoring is safe, not adding earlier warnings and harsher strikes to get approved. It’s doing the opposite in Europe because it has to, and the opposite of that in the US because it can.

We’ve been saying it for a while: FSD gets more dangerous as it gets better, because people trust it more and watch the road less. The answer is monitoring that tightens as the system improves. Europe is forcing exactly that. In the US, Tesla is loosening it, encouraging illegal phone use from the top, and leaving drivers with 100% of the liability when it goes wrong.

Sources indicate that so here’s the question for Tesla. If European owners are getting earlier warnings and instant strikes, why not American owners on the exact same software? Or is NHTSA going to have to force it?

  • Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a blueprint centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”.

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he mentioned.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

Industry observers note that A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he remarked. “What I was doing was not working.”.

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

In a recent development, during ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

Recent findings suggest that “Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”.

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin remarked he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

It has been revealed that ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin remarked BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” noted Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”.

Industry observers note that in March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that when Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

Industry observers note that while the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

Industry observers note that what surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

Recent findings suggest that “I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”.

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a newly introduced way of eating.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he stated. “I still have it for meals.”.

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

Sources indicate that “I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler noted. “I’m not kidding you.”.

According to recent reports, he’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he remarked.

It has been revealed that although he retired from his profession, Bichler mentioned he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he mentioned.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

According to recent reports, “I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

Sources indicate that if you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative upcoming headphones and earbuds have been announced, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

First up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the new Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

The 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously announced $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

As for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

According to recent reports, over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the organization has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

In a recent development, the overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the firm’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

Industry observers note that to ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

Inside Sam Bankman-Fried’s $35 Million Bahamas Crypto HQ

💡 Key Takeaways

  • No matter which retelling you tune into, much of the action is sure to take place at Bankman-Fried’s $35 million “crypto frat house” (as CNBC once called it) in The Bahamas, which served as the headquarters of his cryptocurrency exchange FTX at the time of his and Ellison’s arrests for wire fraud and several conspiracy charges in 2022.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, four years after the fall of cryptocurrency partners-in-crime Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, their Icarian story is coming to the small screen twice over. A docuseries about the scandal, The Boy Who Stole Millions?, debuts on Prime Video November 30, and Netflix’s drama series The Altruists premiered November 19.

No matter which retelling you tune into, much of the action is sure to take place at Bankman-Fried’s $35 million “crypto frat house” (as CNBC once called it) in The Bahamas, which served as the headquarters of his cryptocurrency exchange FTX at the time of his and Ellison’s arrests for wire fraud and several conspiracy charges in 2022.

The Orchid building at Albany, The Bahamas.

Recent findings suggest that bankman-Fried and Ellison met while working at trading firm Jane Street in Manhattan in 2016, and began an on-again, off-again romantic relationship. Bankman-Fried’s first crypto business was the quantitative trading firm he cofounded in 2017, Alameda Research. He went on to found crypto exchange FTX. Ellison, who first began working at Alameda in 2018, became its co-CEO and ran the firm as FTX’s hedge fund.

Bankman-Fried and Ellison moved to The Bahamas in 2021, reportedly motivated by looser COVID-19 pandemic protocols, and “a proactive stance taken by The Bahamas and its regulatory bodies on cryptocurrencies,” Bankman-Fried told Blockworks.

The FTX and Alameda crews encamped at a luxury resort community called Albany. (Tiger Woods and Justin Timberlake are both investors.) Through his companies, Bankman-Fried purchased a penthouse in the sleek Orchid building there, named for its custom cutout façade. Designed by Morris Adjmi Architects, the Orchid’s blue latticework (inspired by Upcoming Orleans ironwork), is unmissable, offering an open-air feel to residents while signaling a layer of privacy to outsiders.

A reception area in the Orchid building.

Bankman-Fried shared his 11,500-square-foot unit with Ellison and eight other FTX and Alameda employees. The apartment has a circular living room, a light-up bar, Italian marble floors, cove lighting, and custom closets. Per a real estate listing obtained by Semafor, Bankman-Fried’s unit had German-engineered windows and doors. Outdoor amenities included a firepit, spa, grill and cooking area, and pool.

It has been revealed that the couple attempted to evade culpability for misappropriating $8 billion of FTX customer money, a crime uncovered after Bankman-Fried bought his Bahamas property. Both were convicted of wire fraud and several conspiracy charges. Ellison served 14 months of a 24-month sentence. Bankman-Fried is presently serving a 25-year prison sentence and maintains that he is innocent.

To bring this story to life for The Altruists, production designer Todd Fjelsted re-created the infamous penthouse. Several interiors were shot in Vancouver, but scenes requiring a beach or docks were shot in the Dominican Republic.

Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison in a scene from The Altruists filmed in the Orchid set.

Fjelsted and his crew also built miniature replicas of real Albany buildings and a marina complete with a 10-foot remote-control yacht, using forced perspective to shoot them as backdrops. He calls this “the anti-AI set.”.

According to recent reports, in the dramatization, coworkers trade crypto in a communal office and party on a balcony overlooking the water. An employee in a hot tub bangs a gong for rounds of speed chess played on fancy sets. Inside, gaming is a major pastime, and there’s a baby grand piano on hand, though no one plays it. In real life, it was reported that Bankman-Fried kept a bean bag under the piano for napping.

Alex Lawther as Sam Trabucco and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

It has been revealed that looking to humanize the leads, Fjelsted observed how “insecurities [and] their feelings of a little bit of an imposter syndrome” informed Sam and Caroline’s design choices or lack thereof. Neutrals, sea colors, and palm tree prints made for a better on-camera look, but in real FBI interior photos, Fjelsted saw bedroom walls with powder blue sponge-painted over navy.

Garner and Boyle as Ellison and Bankman-Fried in The Altruists.

According to recent reports, throughout the show’s eight episodes, the penthouse goes from bustling with the excitement of trading to vibrating with panic as the scandal comes crashing down. Eventually, the space is left nearly empty, with just Bankman-Fried and his parents remaining. In 2024, it was reported that Bankman-Fried’s real estate holdings would be sold off in order to pay back his debts, and today, the unit is indeed up for sale.

The 6 Best Rowing Machines for Your Gym, Tested by Fitness Experts

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • WHEN IT COMES to your fitness routine, it can be nice to switch things up.
  • Indoor rowing is an excellent way to improve cardiovascular fitness and muscular endurance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHEN IT COMES to your fitness routine, it can be nice to switch things up. If you don't own one already, an indoor rowing machine is a piece of equipment you can count on for a high-payoff, low-impact (AKA joint-friendly) workout at home. We've got several in the Men's Health gym, and many of our editors have one or even two at home and use them regularly for this very reason. This might be just the total-body workout you've been looking for.

Indoor rowing is an excellent way to improve cardiovascular fitness and muscular endurance. Since it is a low-impact sport, rowing reduces the risk of damage to weight-bearing joints, such as hips, ankles, and knees, which tend to be prone to injury and soreness when doing high-impact sports. But rowing's not just a great joint-friendly form of cardio. A solid rowing workout can also help build strength in more muscle groups than you'd expect.

Industry observers note that "The rower is basically the horizontal version of the deadlift and uses similar muscles," indicates veteran trainer Ian Creighton. "On the drive, the main focus is on the posterior chain—the hamstrings, glutes, calves, and spinal erectors are all being used. In the pull, the quads, forearms, biceps, and lats are used as well.".

Sources indicate that indoor rowing machines are a bit more complicated than ordinary home gym equipment, like weight benches or dumbbell sets. Decades ago, they used to be little more than a gliding seat and rope handle attached to a water-filled flywheel. But today’s best rowing machines are a lot more high-tech and sophisticated. That’s to say, shopping for a new rower can be a challenge. We’re here to help with the most notable specs, features, and essentials to consider before forking over your hard-earned money. If cost is a major concern, check out our story on the best rowing machines under $500.

Over the past three years, we've tested every major rower on the market, yet the Concept2 RowErg still reigns supreme. Its high-quality construction, easy assembly, and incredibly smooth ride make the RowErg the best in its class. And at this price point, we think it offers many of the same features as the best rowing machines that cost twice as much.

In a recent development, in fact, this piece of home gym equipment is an industry standard used by CrossFit and many high-profile competitions. Our Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, indicates this is his go-to rowing machine because it can blast your abs, glutes, and back while redlining your heart rate. "It's built for either long cardio workouts or vicious high-intensity sessions," he says.

The RowErg has a durable construction that can support people up to 500 pounds. Our editors have used the RowErg in their home gyms for years and found it still works like new. We also appreciate the variable-resistance flywheel, which provides a consistent challenge. Our fitness editors say this feature is especially useful for high-volume use and experienced rowers.

Recent findings suggest that it's easy to assemble, too. In our experience setting up this rower, it takes about 15 minutes, ideally with two people, and minimal tools or hardware (just eight screws). I set mine up myself with no issue, and it took no longer than 10 minutes. Not trying to brag or anything, but it was easy. (I posted a video about the assembly here). Plus, it separates into two pieces for easy storage, making it a great option for people with smaller home gym setups.

It has been revealed that yes, it lacks smart connectivity and the big, beautiful LED screens found in newer models like the Hydrow, but if you're looking for a tough-as-nails machine that can keep up with your toughest workouts, the RowErg delivers the definitive home rowing experience. That's why it's our pick for the best rowing machine of 2026.

Read More: Our Hands-On Review of the Concept2 RowErg.

Sources indicate that "If I can’t use a Concept2, this is my go-to," notes Samuel. The Hydrow Wave is a more streamlined and slimmed-down version of Hydrow's original Rower Connected Rowing Machine—and a 2025 Men's Health Fitness Awards winner. It's a smart machine with an HD screen that features immersive guided workouts to recreate a real-world rowing experience. And after using the Wave Rower for over a year now, we can attest that it delivers on that promise.

Industry observers note that the electromagnetic resistance is incredibly smooth and quiet, and Hydrow's armada of on-demand classes are surprisingly lifelike. "It feels as if you're out on the water, complete with videos shot on lakes and rivers," indicates Samuel. "The end result: a tranquil row seat." While other cardio machines we've tested got repetitive after a few weeks of use, Hydrow's video programs always kept things interesting.

This rower fits easily in my basement training area, and can stand up for storage. Not only does it fold, but it looks good folded up. Despite the compact size, we've found the Wave is also SUPER-durable: I can go hard on this rower for sprints, or take on longer intervals without it struggling to keep up.

We do wish this rower had a free mode to allow customers to build their own workouts. Despite that, this is the best magnetic resistance rowing experience on the market. If you're someone who cares about the details and wants to learn from experts, this is the best pick for you.

Hydrow's pricing is usually the same on Amazon as anywhere else, but if you want to see a full list of add-ons, you might want to purchase one on their website.

Read More: Our Review of the Hydrow Wave Rower.

According to recent reports, whether you're competing live against your peers, trying to out-row world-class athletes, or even being chased by a deadly Kraken, the Strong Series Rower is a fix for boring rowing workouts. Aside from the basics (like tracking performance stats), a massive and crisp definition 22-inch touchscreen allows for streaming content from Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, Prime Video, Spotify, and YouTube, as well as a library of interactive, performance-based video games.

The tech was actually developed by game designers using game psychology, with the singular goal of encouraging rowing performance. The animated games are immersive and easy to learn, and incentivize players to increase output in creative ways.

Aside from the gamified perks, one major feature of this machine is its 20-inch elevated seat, which makes it easy for beginners, older individuals, and those with limited mobility to get on and off the machine. It isn't as low to the ground as more traditional rowing machines, and is therefore more accessible for some people.

The foot pedals are also more wide-set and larger than found on most rowers, which makes it feel more accessible for a range of consumers. For bigger individuals who typically feel crammed or awkward on a standard machine, this is for you. But that doesn't mean it takes up more room. In fact, this rower can be flipped upright easily and stored without a wall mount.

Read More: Exercises to Improve Your Rowing.

Sometimes simpler is just better. The made-in-the-USA design takes things back to basics with a vaguely vintage aesthetic of stained ash wood. There is no denying that in certain homes the aesthetic of a wooden water rower is just superior. This also makes it one of the most heavy-duty machines in this guide, supporting customers up to 700 pounds.

We found that the traditional water-based flywheel not only looks great, but does an incredible job of recreating the feel of rowing through real water. Users can fully customize the resistance by filling the water tank with more or less water, which can make a mess, but isn't difficult to do. Keep in mind you'll also need to treat the water on a consistent basis so it doesn't get moldy.

Recent findings suggest that at around $1,400, this model lacks the fancier gadgetry of the pricier models in our guide. So if you don't rely heavily on video classes or virtual instructors for your motivation then you can save a good amount by going with this simpler machine. Still, the integrated performance monitor tracks all the essentials.

The absence of a screen also means that this piece of equipment can be folded upright and stored easier than most, meaning it's perfect for putting away in closets or corners. For anyone looking for a durable, handsome rower without unnecessary bells and whistles at a good price, this is your pick.

The top-rated Ergatta Rower (a Men's Health Fitness Awards winner) is all performance, complete with game-based workouts that challenge you daily. It's the most "gamified" water-based rowing machine we've tested with a long list of virtual workout programs to choose from. We took it for a spin with head-to-head races, high-intensity endurance workouts, and goal-based gamified training prepares to get the full experience.

Sources indicate that we found this is one of the smoothest water rowers we've used, and the games are enough to keep things fun and interesting even when doing a basic workout. The game-based workouts felt like a much-needed changeup from typical hard workouts on a Concept2, and are actually good for dialing in form.

In a recent development, in terms of the frame, the lone downside is that the feet are positioned a little more closely than we prefer. But on the plus side, rolling this model and folding it is easy. Not only that, but it looks cool even when folded up against the wall.

The warm cherry wood feels extremely durable and gives the rower a sleek retro-modern aesthetic that elevated the look of our home gym space. It's among the priciest rowing machines in this guide, but if you're in the market for a top-of-the-line rower that doubles as a home accessory, it's hard to beat.

Men’s Health fitness writer and strength coach David Otey, CSCS, took the Peloton Cross Training Row+ for a spin and confirmed that it’s set to give every rower in our guide—even the most goated rowing machines—a run for their money.

Sources indicate that otey and MH fitness editors found both the seat and foot pedals extremely comfortable, and the foot strap secure yet easy to adjust with a single hand. Otey describes the strap’s pull as "silky smooth" without the annoying catching found in lesser rowers. We found that the electrically-controlled resistance also makes for whisper-quiet operation.

But the real star isn't its frame. "Peloton's best asset isn't its hardware; it's a great software company," Otey says. The tech on this machine delivers, with a Form Assist function that can help nearly any level rower achieve better form as they row.

Industry observers note that it’s not perfect, however. Otey notes that its most obvious shortcoming is the lack of an adjustable manual mode. This is a stark difference from many manual rowers, which shows Peloton is more confident in their programming and instructors than your ability to create your own workouts.

The rower can be easily stored vertically against a wall, but requires an anchor to go into the wall for safety. This is perfect for any rowers looking for great classes and a well-built machine, especially if they are already Peloton fans.

When considering an indoor rowing machine, you'll encounter a variety of resistance systems.

If you’re dropping $1,000 or more on a complicated piece of gym equipment, you want to know that it can go the distance. That’s why it pays (literally) to buy from a tech giant that you trust and that offers a solid, reputable product with a decent warranty. Don’t settle for a bargain-priced Amazon model from a brand you’ve never heard of just because it seems like a steal. In the world of fitness equipment, you almost always get what you pay for. If you’re planning to row on a regular basis and to keep your rowing machine for the foreseeable future, consider investing good money into a model that will last.

According to recent reports, by their nature, rowing machines are massive, bulky, and often heavy. If you have the real estate in your home, non-folding models are typically sturdier and more convenient when it comes time to work out. They’re always set up and ready to go—er, row. If you’re a city dweller or are just short on space, however, a folding rowing machine might be the best way to go. Some rowers fold neatly in half or offer vertical storage to minimize wasted floor space. Look for models with transport wheels so you can easily move yours around by yourself.

With the best rowing machines priced north of $1,000, buying one is a serious investment. So, it’s notable to purchase from a manufacturer that offers a clear, comprehensive warranty. They vary widely across the industry, with the most budget-forward brands offering just 90 days on some parts, and others boasting generous 10-year warranties on everything. Again, the more you spend upfront, the better the warranty is likely to be. And, if there’s anything that isn’t clear to you about the stated warranty, be sure to ask. It’s your money, after all.

Sources indicate that the most basic rowing machine design has changed little in decades, and you can still find a “classic”-style model for a reasonable price. But, if you’re looking for a more connected experience, look at smart rowers like the Hydrow Wave or the Peloton Row. These offer touchscreens with built-in apps that connect you to professional trainers who can motivate and work with you to better achieve your personal goals. The rowing machines with these features are, of course, more expensive upfront. But, know that many also require ongoing monthly subscriptions to take full advantage of those “smart” connected features.

Industry observers note that as the Fitness and Reviews Editor of Men's Health, it's my job to test the latest and greatest in fitness equipment, including rowing machines. My fellow Men's Health fitness editors and experts included but weren't limited to Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, David Otey, CSCS, and Ian Creighton.

In a recent development, our methodology for assessing the best rowing machines for home use involved thorough testing across performance, build quality, comfort, features, resistance mechanism, and user experience. We conducted extensive performance and stress tests with over two dozen rowing machines through rowing workouts of varying lengths and intensities, and paid close attention to comfort and user-friendly features along the way. We used these rowers through hundreds of miles of testing for warm-ups, cardio burns, HIIT workouts, endurance training, and finishers. Features such as resistance levels, workout programs, and connectivity were scrutinized in detail.

Recent findings suggest that after we had examined each individually, we had our final picks shipped to The Garage Gym in Westfield, New Jersey, to stack them all against each other, literally. Here's our guide to the best rowing machines for your home right now.

Our fitness experts love indoor machines for a ton of reasons. But the biggest one is how easy and accessible they are for enthusiasts of any fitness level. Seriously, there’s not much more to using one than simply sitting down and pulling—rinse and repeat. But like any workout machine, there is a right way and a wrong way. The best way to not only maximize your performance and rowing gains but also to avoid injury is to practice the proper rowing technique.

Start by sitting squarely on the seat with your tailbone pointing directly into the middle. Follow your rowing stroke through each of these four phases, paying careful attention to your posture and form:.

It has been revealed that to start, your shins should be perpendicular to the floor (i.e., vertical). Extend your arms fully—with a focus on your triceps—and grab the rower’s handle. Be mindful of your core, and slightly lean your torso forward.

Recent findings suggest that while keeping your arms straight, power through the Drive phase with your leg muscles, pushing your body (and the seat) smoothly away from the footplates. Finish by pulling the handle into your abdomen and leaning back.

Despite the name, you’re not quite "finished." In this phase, your elbows should be bent and the handle tucked into the lower part of your chest. Use your core to stabilize your torso, keeping a slight angle toward the rowing machine.

According to recent reports, be mindful of your form while returning to the starting position in this phase. Straighten your arms by using your triceps. Slightly lean your torso forward. Bend your legs and smoothly slide your butt and the seat down the rail of the rowing machine.

Once back in the starting position, repeat the next stroke by beginning with the Drive phase again.

Rowing is a near-perfect exercise, and a good indoor rowing machine promises a low-impact, full-body workout with the convenience of a single device. “Since rowing promotes improvements to both your muscular strength and cardiovascular strength, you get two for one,” says Tuttle. She outlines four specific reasons why you should buy a rowing machine:.

“A proper warmup is key to having a successful workout; it should prepare your heart, muscles, joints, and mind for the harder efforts to come,” claims Tuttle. Because it’s so low-impact, it’s a great slow warm-up, even if rowing isn’t your ultimate program goal on a given day.

Because rowing is significantly lower impact than most high-intensity exercises like running, it’s far easier to recover between workouts. Ideally, a rowing machine will help add variety to your workout days.

According to recent reports, because indoor rowing involves fewer external stimuli than outdoor activities, it can be extremely meditative. Tuttle agrees: “Once warm and a comfortable rhythm has been established, you can close your eyes, connect your breath to your body, and simply enjoy the gift of movement,” she claims.

Hardcore workout sessions often involve an explosive finish. Hopping on your rowing machine near the end of your routine is a great way to cap things off. “It's hard to pass up a good 5- to 10-minute long EMOM (Every Minute On the Minute) row 100 to 200 meters, depending upon your fitness and skill level,” claims Tuttle. “Each effort should be about 90 percent max intensity and your goal is to finish with 20 seconds or more to recover before the top of the next minute.”.

According to recent reports, if a low-impact cardio machine is what you're looking for, it's true that indoor bikes and rowers can both be suitable options. The best choice for you? Well, it all comes down to your goals.

The rowing machine provides a full-body workout that engages multiple muscle groups. However, it requires a technique and coordination to avoid injury and that can be less intuitive for some consumers compared to using an exercise bike. Rowers also take up more space and can be noisy.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, stationary bikes can provide a great cardio workout, are more adjustable (seat height, handlebars, etc.) and are easy to use. But biking primarily focuses on lower-body muscles, and may not challenge the upper body or coordination as effectively as a rowing machine.

In general, states Samuel, the rower will be the more advanced cardio option. According to him, the rower delivers a more “well-rounded” workout. It also directly challenges your mid-back muscles, lower back muscles, and glutes.

“These are all key postural muscles,” Samuel told us, “so you’re getting extra benefits out of the rower.”.

The downside: Rowing also requires more technique, so there’s a higher learning curve to dominating on the rower.

The best way to avoid getting injured on the rower is to master proper technique, according to Samuel. You'll want to tighten your abs before each pull, and aim to let your legs drive the motion. He recommends working hard not to lean back too aggressively as you finish each row stroke; think of your torso shifting between a 10 o'clock angle and 2 o'clock as you row. Anything more than that isn't beneficial.

It has been revealed that additionally, start every row workout with a brief warmup. This doesn't need to take long, but before you start pulling to the max during any workout, spend at least a minute doing slower, controlled pulls through the full range of your rowing motion, driving blood flow and gradually elevating your heart rate. That'll get you primed to row your best.

According to recent reports, finally, make sure there's plenty of room on every side of the rower. Having three feet of space on either side of the rower will allow you to comfortably pull your arms backward even if your elbows flare. You'll want five to seven feet behind the rower, giving you room to shift your torso backward on every stride. And keep a few feet in front of the rower, too. And remember, if you're rowing hard, your heart rate will climb up there. So, don’t forget a decent cool-down.

Targeted fat loss has been proven to be virtually impossible. But rowing machines are great for almost every aspect of fitness, including building strength, lowering overall body fat, increasing stamina, and even weight loss. The reason is simple: By burning a ton of calories (putting yourself in a calorie deficit), you can more easily score a negative daily energy balance. Bottom line: You’re consuming fewer calories than you’re burning. Maintaining a calorie deficit over a long period is the guiding principle behind successfully losing weight and keeping it off.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England.
  • The sex and weight have not been confirmed yet, and the calf also does not have a name.
  • At birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage shows rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been confirmed yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

At birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

The team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help plan out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she demonstrated signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos remarked in an e-mailed statement. “It was a big moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”.

According to recent reports, both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

“Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”.

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Presently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

Recent findings suggest that while the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species presently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This fresh calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

“Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Kia Besta EV hit the roads in 1986 as the brand’s first fully electric vehicle. 40 years later, Kia continues to “lead the pack” with a full lineup of EVs ranging from entry-level cars and SUVs to three-row models, and just about everything in between.

Kia wanted to design a fresh vehicle for the 1986 Asian Games, which were held in Seoul, South Korea, one that did not emit any toxic fumes in front of runners.

So, it created the Besta EV. The Besta van was initially developed 40 years ago by Kia’s Central Research Institute as the successor to the popular Bongo van, which is still sold in Korea and other markets today.

Unlike the Bongo, it was developed using Kia’s in-house tech rather than sourced from another automaker and rebadged as its own.

Kia swapped the 2.0L four-cylinder diesel engine for a 35 kWh battery and electric motor, which provided a range of more than 26 miles (42 km) on a single charge.

While the Besta EV was never actually sold to the public, it laid the groundwork and offered an early glimpse at Kia’s shift to electrification.

Sources indicate that the first mass-produced Korean EV certified for commercial sale was the Kia Pride EV in 1993. In 2011, the Ray EV became Kia’s first series-production electric car.

Kia expanded its electrification ambitions to Europe and the UK in 2014 with the first-generation Soul EV, the beloved boxy, funky crossover that was discontinued after the 2025 model year.

The Korean automaker has come a long way since the Besta EV, with a full lineup of electric vehicles ranging from compact cars to mid-size and three-row SUVs, vans, and just about everything in between.

Kia now offers an electric option for nearly everyone with seven-passenger EVs on sale in the UK and Europe, including the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 Passenger van.

Sources indicate that with its first software-defined vehicle (SDV) and a new B-segment electric hatchback set to launch by the end of 2027, Kia has no plans to slow down. On top of this, Kia will expand its PBV lineup with the PV7 next year, a larger sibling to the PV5.

Four decades after the Besta EV arrived, Kia said it continues to “lead the pack today” with one of the most diverse all-electric EV lineups of any brand.

Through October, Kia has sold over 135,000 EVs in the UK, with fully electric vehicles now accounting for over 37% of total sales.

Thanks to its latest EV lineup, Kia became “Europe’s fastest-growing top 10 passenger-car brand.” According to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Kia registered 377,078 vehicles between January and August 2026, up 9% compared to the same period last year.

Sjoerd Knipping, Chief Operating Officer of Kia Europe, noted the growth is thanks to having “one of the broadest and most advanced electrified line-ups in Europe.”.

Industry observers note that in the US, Kia released the compact EV3 (check out our review of it) this year, starting at just $29,890. It joins the EV6, EV9, and Niro EV in Kia’s US electric vehicle lineup.

You don't need much of an imagination to picture yourself curled up on one of 7th Avenue's sectionals.
