Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that but no one else would.
  • Industry observers note that it worked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S. government to stop supersonic jets. By day, the Harvard-trained physicist ran experiments at the Cambridge Electron Accelerator. By night, he spent hours writing letters—to congressmen, federal aviation officials, mayors, and newspaper editors. It was not a job he wanted. “I was hoping and praying someone else would do it,” he told The Harvard Crimson.

Sources indicate that but no one else would. So Shurcliff launched the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S. commercial aviation history at the time, the Supersonic Transport (SST) program. His opposition to the SST stemmed from research by Swedish scientist Bo Lundberg, who had written extensively on the perils of supersonic aviation, chiefly the sonic boom, which could impact hundreds of millions of people every day. Shurcliff’s goal was uncompromising. “Just as the only way to get rid of the smell of the skunk is to eliminate the skunk,” he told The Latest York Times, “we propose to attack the sonic boom by eliminating the SST.”.

Industry observers note that it worked. In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S. soil.

Sources indicate that today, prompted by a 2025 executive order, the FAA is proposing to lift that ban before any community response tests of emerging supersonic technology have taken place. And even if latest engineering designs can reduce the sonic booms at airliner scale, the economic and environmental costs that have plagued supersonic flight haven’t changed since Shurcliff’s day.

During World War II, Shurcliff worked at the federal Office of Scientific Research and Development, helping keep the Manhattan Project’s atomic-bomb patents secret. In 1946, he witnessed firsthand the atomic tests at Bikini Atoll and wrote the official account, Bombs at Bikini. His son later told The Fresh York Times that his father was so affected he spent the rest of his life atoning for that work.

Sources indicate that when supersonic aviation programs began heating up in the 1960s, Shurcliff was wary of the press, but he was clear about supersonic technology. “We all believe in progress,” he told the Crimson, “but some things just aren’t progress.”.

In a recent development, the U.S. government-sponsored SST program was the culmination of supersonic military research that began on the heels of World War II. In January 1947, months before anyone had flown faster than sound, Popular Science described Bell’s experimental XS-1, also known as the X-1, which it remarked might someday reach 1,700 mph, more than twice the speed of sound and three times faster than a typical commercial jet. That October, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in the X-1.

Fifteen years later, in 1962, Britain and France agreed to build Concorde, and the Soviet Union soon launched its own supersonic airliner program, Tupolev Tu-144. The following year, President John F. Kennedy committed the U.S. to a faster, bigger rival, SST. Boeing won the contract in 1966. But even as the race heated up, an enormous problem trailed in its wake.

It has been revealed that sit in a closed room and the air feels perfectly still, but it isn’t. At room temperature, air molecules zip around at an average of about 1,000 miles per hour, each one bouncing off its neighbors billions of times a second. You don’t feel a gale because they’re flying every which way at once—for every molecule headed toward your face, another is headed away. What you’re feeling, without noticing, is the sum of all that pummeling—air pressure—about 14.7 pounds of it on every square inch (psi) of your body at sea level. You notice it only when the balance shifts, such as when the wind blows—a mass of air being pushed from high pressure toward low.

That restless jostling of air molecules is also how sound travels. A voice, a drumbeat, or a jet engine will shove the molecules, which pass along the shove like a crowd in a stadium passing along a wave even as every fan stays in place. The ricocheting molecules pass along vibrations somewhat inefficiently, which is why sound travels a bit slower than the molecules themselves, about 760 mph at sea level, and slower still in the frigid air at airplane cruising altitudes.

When a plane flies faster than the speed of sound, it outruns the air molecules carrying the wave. The air ahead gets no warning until the jet slams it aside, compressing it and creating a shock wave that trails the jet like the V-shaped wake behind a speedboat. But the shock wave’s wake is three-dimensional, spreading in a widening cone that sweeps across the ground below.

According to recent reports, A sonic boom isn’t a single bang that occurs the moment a plane “breaks the sound barrier.” It’s a continuous swath of jarring noise and pressure that follows the jet. Anyone in the cone’s path, or “boom carpet,” experiences it.

In his 1970 explainer, S/S/T and Sonic Boom Handbook, Shurcliff estimated the boom carpet at 40 to 60 miles wide for the supersonic aircraft of his day. The jolt hits hardest directly beneath the flight path and weakens toward the cone’s edges.

Worse, Shurcliff warned, boom behavior was erratic. Swirls of wind and temperature could focus a shock wave so that one house took twice the jolt of its neighbor a few hundred feet away. That, he argued, meant people would never get used to sonic booms, just as people never get used to lightning and thunder.

On paper, booms don’t seem like they should be a major deal. A boom from supersonic passenger jets like Concorde raises air pressure at sea level about .014 psi relative to the normal 14.7 psi we live with—that’s just a 0.1 percent increase. It doesn’t seem like much, but relative to everyday sounds, it’s enormous.

It has been revealed that if you’ve ever stood near the speakers at a live concert and felt the bass or drum hit your chest, you’ve felt a pressure pulse like a sonic boom, but that bass is only 6.5 pascals, or Pa, a measure of air pressure. Now multiply that punch by about 15 and deliver it without warning. It’s roughly the shove of a 30 mph wind gust delivered in a fraction of a second and aimed at every wall and window of your house at once. That’s what the 0.1 percent of a supersonic jet actually represents.

It has been revealed that what no one knew in the early 1960s, when supersonic research was barreling ahead, was how people would feel living under that boom carpet day after day. In 1964, the FAA decided to find out, picking Oklahoma City.

It has been revealed that in a six-month trial that began in February 1964, Oklahoma City residents were subjected to eight sonic booms a day, starting at 7 a.m., to gauge how well they would accept the disruption, and whether they would grow accustomed to it. By the end, the Oklahoma City Council had requested a halt to the flights, and the FAA had logged more than 12,000 calls, mostly complaints, alongside more than 5,000 damage claims for broken windows, cracked walls and floors, and destruction of personal property.

Industry observers note that despite the fallout, the following year the agency pointed to a University of Chicago survey of Oklahoma City residents as vindication. Nearly three-quarters stated they could live with eight booms a day indefinitely. The survey’s own numbers told a different story.

Nearly every resident surveyed, 94 percent, reported rattling walls and windows, and almost four in 10 believed the booms had damaged their homes. The longer the booms continued, the less people liked them. The share who felt more than a little annoyed rose from 37 percent to 56 percent, and those who mentioned they could live with the booms fell from 91 percent to 73 percent during the six-month trial. Anger over the FAA’s handling of damage claims eventually turned Oklahoma Senator Mike Monroney, one of aviation’s staunchest champions, against the SST program.

It has been revealed that although the residents of Oklahoma City delivered mixed results, the negative data emboldened the opposition. Shurcliff debuted the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom (CLASB) in March 1967 with a handful of friends and colleagues. Their mission was to eliminate the SST program and keep its boom out of American skies. By June, CLASB had about 230 members in 18 states. What united them, Shurcliff told The Newly introduced York Times, was that they were “human beings who don’t like to be hit over our heads without our permission being asked.”.

Industry observers note that SST opposition grew as the fight dragged on. Environmental groups joined in, along with economists who doubted the SST would ever pay for itself. For a man upcoming to public relations, Shurcliff seized the moment, casting sonic booms in the language of a rising environmental movement, calling them “sonic pollution.” Atmospheric scientists began warning that SST’s high-altitude exhaust could erode the ozone layer.

Sources indicate that in 1971, Congress finally voted to cut off the program’s funding, ending America’s bid for a supersonic passenger airliner. But across the Atlantic, the European program was forging ahead.

In 1963, a plane flew to space. Why couldn’t we go farther?

In 1934, Chrysler bet big on teardrop-shaped cars.

Sources indicate that robotaxis almost happened in 1964—with help from the U.S. government.

In 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?

During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’.

Industry observers note that in 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.

Concorde began carrying paying passengers in January 1976, cruising at twice the speed of sound and crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. But the U.S. overland ban confined it mostly to ocean routes. Only British Airways and Air France, both state-owned at the time, ever flew Concorde’s small fleet.

In July 2000, an Air France Concorde flight crashed on takeoff outside Paris, killing everyone aboard and halting flights for more than a year. In February 2002, Popular Science writer Bill Sweetman called the crash not only a tragedy but also “a metaphor for the sorry state of supersonic air travel.” But he also reported that a new supersonic race had “quietly” begun.

Recent findings suggest that private-jet maker Gulfstream wanted “a passenger jet for the rich that can smash the sound barrier yet is quiet enough to fly anywhere, anytime.” Controlling the boom was the chief obstacle. But in August 2003, over the California desert, a modified Northrop Grumman F-5 fighter plane demonstrated that a sonic boom could be reshaped and softened.

Two months later, Concorde made its last commercial flight, officially ending the supersonic era for passenger airliners.

The modern darling of supersonic flight is NASA’s X-59, a one-seat research jet built by Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works. With a tapered nose that stretches roughly a third of its length, the plane’s shape spreads the shock waves so they reach the ground as a thump rather than a boom. The X-59 first flew in October 2025, went supersonic in June 2026, and a week later reached its target of Mach 1.4, or roughly 925 mph at 55,000 feet. Next, NASA prepares to fly it over U.S. communities and ask residents how the thumps sound to them. In effect, we’re gearing up for Oklahoma City again, six decades later, albeit, with a gentler jolt.

Sources indicate that since Concorde’s retirement, a handful of private supersonic startups have come, and mostly gone. Denver-based Boom Supersonic flew its one-third-scale XB-1 demonstrator faster than sound three times in January 2025, claiming that no audible boom reached the ground. Its engineering innovation is to exploit atmospheric physics. Since sound travels faster in warm air near the ground than in the frigid air up high, a jet flying only slightly faster than sound at altitude is effectively flying slower than sound near the surface. So its shock waves bend back upward before they land, a phenomenon called Mach cutoff. Boom’s planned Overture jet, seating 60 to 80 passengers, would cruise at Mach 1.7 over oceans—leaving booms in its wake—but just above Mach 1 over land, where their booms would never be heard on the ground, just the distant rumble of their jet engines. The plane hasn’t been built, and its engine is still in development.

But Washington isn’t waiting for the data. A June 2025 executive order directed the FAA to repeal its 1973 sonic boom ban over land. In July 2026, the agency proposed a replacement. Civilian jets, both commercial and private, could fly supersonic over U.S. soil as long as their booms register no more than 0.11 pounds per square foot on the ground, about a twentieth of Concorde’s. That’s about 5 Pa, or slightly less than the pressure felt standing next to the speakers at a live concert (6.5 Pa). But airlines, airports, and Europe’s aviation regulator have questioned whether enough evidence supports the number, which the FAA set without the X-59 having flown over a single community.

Even if the boom fades to a thump, the environmental cost doesn’t. Flying faster than sound means fighting far more drag. According to a 2018 analysis by the International Council on Clean Transportation, a new supersonic airliner would “burn five to seven times as much fuel per passenger as a comparable subsonic jet.” Boom Supersonic states Overture will be able to run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, but airlines, not manufacturers, decide what goes in the tank.

As Popular Science’s Bill Sweetman wrote in 2002, if you can afford a supersonic jet, “you’re not worried about a few lousy tons of fuel.” But everyone below will bear the cost of supersonic jetsetters’ small travel-time benefit in excess noise and climate-warming emissions.

Sources indicate that shurcliff saw this attempt to relax the rules coming. “Once they start flying, they’re going to want to fly them everywhere,” he told The Latest York Times in 1967, warning that over-water routes would be “like a foot in the door.” Fifty-nine years later, thanks to the FAA, the door is swinging open. It’s up to us to decide whether we’re prepared to live with the repercussions or push back as Shurcliff did more than half a century ago.

The Volkswagen ID. Buzz Beach is an electric van built for camping, but it’s not cheap

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that volkswagen introduced the ID.
  • Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.
  • Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that volkswagen introduced the ID. Buzz Beach, a fun spin on its electric van that’s built for camping and overnight stays. However, it won’t be cheap, starting at over $70,000.

Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.

The ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-new style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.

Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a fresh member to the electric people mover lineup.

According to recent reports, the latest ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen noted after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.

Volkswagen stated it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.

The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.

In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.

Sources indicate that for camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a new Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.

It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.

According to recent reports, the ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.

To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.

It has been revealed that volkswagen will open orders for the newly introduced ID. Buzz Beach in the UK later this month, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it will start at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.

Nice product at the wrong price. If VW can't lower the price because of the cost, then it has a lot more work to do to compete in this market.

What about those in the US? VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with a new Tourer model that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.

However, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be delaying the ID. Buzz’s return until the 2028 model year.

The 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.

Sources indicate that A custom camper variant would likely cost more than $70,000. Would you pay $70,000 or more for Volkswagen’s electric camper van?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died.
  • The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.
  • He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”.

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Firm, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

According to recent reports, alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

According to recent reports, lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth.
  • William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.
  • In a recent development, “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 18. Since takes about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA officially confirmed that it reached the distance on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

In a recent development, “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he says. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”.

Astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 miles per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

But even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

Sources indicate that “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” Dave Gallagher, the director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, remarked in an emailed statement confirming the milestone. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

Even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

“Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” indicates Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”.

“Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two newly introduced Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

Recent findings suggest that as part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

All good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are presently operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical problems, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

Industry observers note that “Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any upcoming region.”.

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an notable lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

Recent findings suggest that “Do not be afraid to dream significant. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he notes. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”.

Sources indicate that UPDATE November 19 10:00 a.m. EST: An earlier version of this story remarked light moves at 186,282 feet per second. It is 186,282 miles per second. We have updated unit of measurement and apologize for the error.

#132853. Netflix’s The Altruists Tells a Compelling Story of Love, Money, and Fraud. Here’s What Really Happened.

Netflix’s The Altruists Tells a Compelling Story of Love, Money, and Fraud. Here’s What Really Happened.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, NETFLIX’S LATEST HEADLINE-MAKING limited series The Altruists has a lot of significant names attached to it.
  • It has been revealed that who, you ask?
  • Why is this story about fraud (of which Bankman-Fried was eventually convicted) called The Altruists?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, NETFLIX’S LATEST HEADLINE-MAKING limited series The Altruists has a lot of significant names attached to it. There are Irish and American actors Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner, respectively, playing up their dorkiest selves to portray Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison. (Ostensibly while Garner desperately awaits casting in a possible Madonna biopic that has been in development hell for what feels like forever.).

It has been revealed that who, you ask? Well, if you’ve avoided the cryptocurrency market and carbon-positive NFT gorillas in the past several years, we can’t really blame you. But what you need to know is that Bankman-Fried and Ellison were the heads of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX as well as lovers. FTX, and the love between them, notoriously collapsed when Bankman-Fried was arrested and accused of stealing over $8 billion in customer funds.

Why is this story about fraud (of which Bankman-Fried was eventually convicted) called The Altruists? Ironically, FTX was purportedly created as a company that gave away as much as it earned, based on the principle of effective altruism—words that got everyone in the finance world hot and heavy with excitement. Until news came out that Bankman-Fried and other FTX executives had spent billion-dollar-sized wads of cash “on luxury hotel stays, private planes, DoorDash orders, trips to Jimmy Buffett's Margaritaville, and, in the case of one top executive, a $2.5 million yacht,” Business Insider reports. FTX was also known for hosting an ultra-luxe conference in the Bahamas that featured famous folks including Bill Clinton, Tom Brady, and the musicians Steve Aoki and the late Liam Payne of One Direction, who in 2024 fell to his death from a hotel balcony in Argentina at the age of 31.

So, yeah, we’re dealing with a twisted and extremely millennial story full of curveballs and screwballs. But whether you’re watching The Altruists or simply hearing about it, what do you need to know about the true FTX story at the heart of it? We’ve got you covered below.

The Altruists is as much a love story as it is a story of financial doom: The two were intertwined with Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, who met at an investment firm and fell in love. Bankman-Fried would found FTX as well as its sister cryptocurrency trading firm Alameda Research, while Ellison was CEO of Alameda Research, which funneled money from FTX.

FTX was on an upward trajectory in the early 2020s, garnering Bankman-Fried the nickname of “Crypto King.” The tech giant, once worth $32 billion, nosedived into bankruptcy in 2022 while also being investigated by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Justice Department. Bankman-Fried “sounded surprisingly calm” in an interview with The Latest York Times amid FTX’s freefall. “You would’ve thought that I’d be getting no sleep right now, and instead I’m getting some,” he told the publication. “It could be worse.”.

Yes. In fact, things could and did get a lot worse for this once seemingly altruistic finance dude. He and Ellison broke off their romantic relationship amid FTX’s collapse in 2022. (“She wanted more from it than I was able to give,” Bankman-Fried testified, according to the Wall Street Journal. To which one can only wonder: More than $8 billion?).

On March 28, 2024, Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and was additionally ordered to “pay $11 billion in forfeiture for his orchestration of multiple fraudulent schemes,” the Justice Department confirmed.

In total, he was convicted of two counts of wire fraud, two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering.

What’s curious is that his right-hand woman, Ellison, only got less than two years in prison for her part in the cryptocurrency fraud, though she did plead guilty to two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, two counts of wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit commodities fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. She was also ordered to forfeit $11 billion.

In a recent development, her relatively light sentence can be explained by the fact that, though the “very math-y” Stanford graduate helped orchestrate the multibillion-dollar scheme alongside Bankman-Fried, she became a star witness for the prosecution against her former boyfriend. The prosecutors offered her a sweetened deal to shorten her prison time in exchange for cooperation, information, and testimony.

In a recent development, she testified, NPR reports, that as Alameda found itself in a financial hole, Bankman-Fried directed her to take more money from FTX customers to bail the firm out. “We were in a bad situation,” she said.

Industry observers note that U.S. Attorney Damian Williams said of Bankman-Fried’s scheme that it was “one of the largest financial frauds in history, stealing over $8 billion of his customers’ money.”.

Sources indicate that their love may be over, and they are both convicted felons, all of which gets packed into the final episode of the eight-part The Altruists. But at least Ellison is moving on. Sort of. After being imprisoned for less than two years, she is now a free woman.

Industry observers note that in September, Ellison formally joined Manifund “to develop our funding platform and research how to effectively direct philanthropic dollars,” the company’s CEO Austin Chen unveiled, per Oxygen. She had reportedly joined the nonprofit funding platform and philanthropic organization on a trial basis at first and went by the innocent-sounding pseudonym “Carol.” This work is in line with her stated belief in effective altruism, which in turn became a multibillion-dollar con, which doesn’t sound all that altruistic or effective.

“On FTX itself, I remain conflicted. It was their money and spirit that enabled the Future Fund, and I still admire many aspects of FTX and the individuals who worked there,” Chen wrote. “But also: FTX did wrong. Its collapse harmed users (myself included), and damaged the movement which I deeply care about.”.

Chen is a substantial believer in redemption. “I’d like to give her the opportunity to contribute back to the world,” he wrote. “I hope that the world will concur.” Which is very generous of him. Maybe she’ll even get a Nathan Fielder-hosted documentary one day.

Industry observers note that bankman-Fried, meanwhile? He’s still behind bars on that 25-year sentence. Thankfully for him, however, he is incarcerated at the low-security California federal prison Federal Correctional Institution Lompoc, which is known for its open dormitory and room-type housing.

According to recent reports, maybe he will find a fresh way to be altruistic. Or, at least, stop committing federal crimes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, wandering through the ruins of Pompeii, the ancient Roman city frozen in time by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, one is struck by that civilization’s devotion to precious materials. Surviving mosaics depict the opulence that once filled the city’s lavish homes. These fragments of classical life, and the richness with which they were rendered, captured the imagination of Polish-born designer Daniel Kolodziejczak, inspiring his upcoming Tesserae series for the Newly introduced York design gallery Ateliers Courbet.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz.

Sun hits a pendant in rock crystal and smoky quartz.

Kolodziejczak creates objects in marble, precious stones, and bronze at his workshop in Carrara, Italy.

Sources indicate that kolodziejczak, who started as a jewelry designer in Paris for brands like Givenchy and Saint Laurent, began making decorative objects and furniture after a move to Milan. His exhibition at Ateliers Courbet (on view until January 16, 2027) was inspired by fragments of leftover stone he found in the marble yards of Carrara, not far from his workshop. “Every time I go there I find myself buying new stones,” Kolodziejczak claims.

Kolodziejczak with two vessels from his Tesserae series.

A vessel in rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz.

The designer polishes the base to a console from his Tesserae series.

The remnants accumulated in his studio until, on a visit to Pompeii, he had “the idea to bring them together” in one exhibition. His vessel shapes, inspired by antique Roman pottery, are hand-carved in marble, along with materials like rock crystal, smoky quartz, and citrine quartz. The series will also include a monumental crystal pendant light, sconces in bronze with citrine quartz shades, a mirror, and massive stone tables. But despite the expansive scale, Kolodziejczak’s sensibility remains rooted in the concept of adornment. “I treat furniture like jewelry,” claims the designer, whose Studio Daniel K is based in Milan and Paris. “These pieces aren’t meant to take up the entire room—just to be that accent of something extraordinary.”.
